traditions.name: Jōmon
traditions.visualCaption: Fire and cord. 16,000 years of making.

story.hook: The oldest pottery on Earth wasn't made for beauty—it was made for survival.
story.body: Sixteen thousand years ago, someone in what is now Japan pressed twisted cord into wet clay. They couldn't have known they were inventing one of humanity's most enduring art forms. Jōmon means 'cord-marked,' and these vessels—with their wild, flame-like rims and deeply textured surfaces—remain some of the most expressive ceramics ever made. The famous 'flame vessels' of the Middle Jōmon period feature elaborate sculptural rims that seem to dance with fire itself. These weren't decorative objects; they were cooking pots, burial urns, ritual vessels. The Jōmon people were hunter-gatherers who stayed in one place long enough to need—and make—pottery. Every piece was coiled by hand, fired in open pits at relatively low temperatures. The surfaces hold fingerprints, cord impressions, the marks of shells and bamboo.
story.reflection: What does it mean that the oldest pottery feels so contemporary?

traditions.name: Buncheong
traditions.visualCaption: Freedom in slip. Korea's happy accident.

story.hook: For 200 years, Korean potters made what might be the most joyful ceramics in history.
story.body: Buncheong emerged in 15th-century Korea as celadon traditions loosened their grip. Regional potters, freed from court standards, began to play. They brushed white slip loosely over dark clay, scratched fish and birds with abandon, stamped patterns with cheerful repetition. The results were whimsical, earthy, sophisticated, and utterly Korean. When Japan invaded Korea in the 1590s, hundreds of Korean potters were taken to Japan, where buncheong aesthetics transformed Japanese tea ceremony ware. In Korea, the tradition vanished, replaced by white porcelain. It wasn't until the 20th century that Korean artists rediscovered buncheong—and found in its gestural freedom something that felt startlingly like abstract expressionism.
story.reflection: What happens when you let go of refinement and embrace the gestural?

traditions.name: Raku
traditions.visualCaption: Pulled from fire. Made for tea.

story.hook: A tile maker's son created bowls for the most powerful man in Japan—and invented an aesthetic that would change ceramics forever.
story.body: In 16th-century Kyoto, Sen no Rikyū was transforming the tea ceremony into something radical: stripped of ostentation, focused on humble materials and moments of profound attention. He needed bowls to match his vision. He found Chōjirō, son of a tile maker, who created vessels so simple they were revolutionary. These black and red bowls—hand-formed, not wheel-thrown, pulled hot from the kiln—became known as Raku, from a seal meaning 'enjoyment' or 'ease.' The Raku family has passed down this tradition for 15 generations. Western Raku, developed in the 20th century, takes the technique in different directions—post-firing reduction, metallic lusters, crackled surfaces—but the core remains: direct relationship with fire, the mark of the maker's hand, acceptance of the unexpected.
story.reflection: What would it mean to make something worthy of profound attention?

traditions.name: Barro Negro
traditions.visualCaption: Polished darkness. 2,000 years of black clay.

story.hook: In a village in Oaxaca, they've been making midnight from mud for two millennia.
story.body: San Bartolo Coyotepec is a village built on black clay. For over 2,000 years, Zapotec potters have transformed this local material into vessels of such deep, lustrous black that they seem to absorb light. The secret is reduction firing—starving the kiln of oxygen so carbon penetrates the clay. Then burnishing: rubbing the surface with quartz stones until it gleams like obsidian. Doña Rosa Real de Nieto revolutionized the tradition in the 1950s, developing new forms and achieving unprecedented shine. Today her descendants and neighbors continue the work, each family with its own style. The pottery is made entirely by hand—no wheel, no glaze, just clay, fire, and patient polishing.
story.reflection: What could you make from the clay beneath your own feet?

image.alt: Barro Negro (Barro Negro y normal-San Bartolo Coyotepec-Oaxaca-Mexico)

traditions.name: Celadon
traditions.visualCaption: Jade made from earth. The color of heaven.

story.hook: For a thousand years, potters chased a color that existed only in their imagination.
story.body: The color of celadon has been called 'the color of the sky after rain,' 'the green of young bamboo,' 'the gray-green of weathered jade.' It's none of these and all of them—a color that seems to shift with the light, to hold depth like water. Chinese potters developed celadon glazes by the 10th century, seeking to imitate precious jade. Korean potters of the Goryeo dynasty (918-1392) took the tradition to unprecedented heights, developing the sanggam technique—carving designs into the clay and filling them with white and black slip before glazing. The result: images of cranes, clouds, and willow trees floating beneath the jade-green surface.
story.reflection: What color would you chase for a thousand years?

image.credit: Iwanafish at English Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons

traditions.name: Majolica
traditions.visualCaption: Stories on tin. Mediterranean color.

story.hook: In Renaissance Italy, potters learned to paint myths on breakfast dishes.
story.body: Majolica began as a technology: tin-opacified glaze that created a brilliant white surface perfect for painting. The technique traveled from the Islamic world through Spain to Italy, where Renaissance potters transformed it into high art. Urbino and Faenza became centers of istoriato ware—elaborate narrative scenes covering entire plates, painted in brilliant cobalt blue, copper green, manganese purple, and antimony yellow. Every plate told a story: classical myths, biblical scenes, contemporary events. The tradition spread to Spain and then to Mexico, where indigenous potters merged it with pre-Columbian traditions to create Talavera.
story.reflection: What story would you paint on a plate?

traditions.name: Mingei
traditions.visualCaption: Beauty of use. The hand of the unknown craftsman.

story.hook: A philosopher looked at humble rice bowls and saw a new way of understanding beauty.
story.body: In the 1920s, Yanagi Sōetsu was studying Korean Yi dynasty ceramics when he had a revelation. The beauty he found in these everyday vessels—made quickly, without self-consciousness, for use—was different from the beauty of fine art. He called it mingei, the 'art of the people.' Yanagi's idea was radical: true beauty emerged not from individual genius but from the unselfconscious repetition of traditional forms. He gathered a circle of potters—Shoji Hamada, Kanjiro Kawai, Bernard Leach—who would transform this philosophy into a movement.
story.reflection: What could you make if you weren't trying to make art?

image.alt: Mingei (Thrown, Combed tea bowl by Shoji Hamada (YORYM-2004.1.1957) (cropped))

traditions.name: Shigaraki
traditions.visualCaption: Fire and ash. One of Japan's Six Ancient Kilns.

story.hook: In the hills near Kyoto, potters have been dancing with fire for 800 years.
story.body: Shigaraki is one of Japan's Six Ancient Kilns—production centers with continuous ceramic traditions stretching back to the Kamakura period. The local clay, rich in feldspar, creates a distinctive warm orange body with a rough, sandy texture. But Shigaraki's signature is what the kiln does: natural ash from the wood fire settles on pieces during the long firing, creating drips and patterns that no human hand could plan. Tea masters prized these 'fire marks' and 'kiln effects.' Each piece records its unique journey through the kiln.
story.reflection: What if you let the fire do some of the work?

traditions.name: Delftware
traditions.visualCaption: Dutch blue. Imitating China, becoming itself.

story.hook: When Chinese porcelain stopped arriving, Dutch potters invented their own version—and created something entirely new.
story.body: In the early 17th century, the Dutch East India Company flooded European markets with Chinese blue-and-white porcelain. Then civil war disrupted Chinese production, and suddenly there was a gap in the market. Potters in Delft stepped in, creating tin-glazed earthenware painted to imitate the Chinese imports. Yet something happened in the translation. Chinese motifs mixed with Dutch sensibilities. Windmills appeared alongside pagodas. Tulips bloomed beside peonies. Eventually, distinctly Dutch imagery dominated.
story.reflection: What happens when you stop imitating and start creating?

image.alt: Delftware (Vase, c. 1680, Delft, Netherlands, tin-glazed earthenware - Art Institute of Chicago - DSC)

traditions.name: African Coil Pottery
traditions.visualCaption: Earth and fire. Hands across millennia.

story.hook: Across Africa, women have been shaping clay with their hands for ten thousand years.
story.body: African ceramic traditions are as diverse as the continent itself, but many share common threads: coiling and pinching rather than wheel-throwing, burnishing rather than glazing, pit-firing rather than kilns, and often, women as the primary makers. In many cultures, pottery-making knowledge passes from mother to daughter, carrying not just technique but spiritual significance. Contemporary African ceramicists like Magdalene Odundo and Andile Dyalvane draw on these traditions while pushing into new territory.
story.reflection: What knowledge might your hands carry from your ancestors?

traditions.name: Iznik
traditions.visualCaption: Ottoman splendor. Cobalt, turquoise, and sealing-wax red.

story.hook: In a small town near Istanbul, potters created some of the most stunning ceramics the world has ever seen—then lost the secret forever.
story.body: Iznik ware represents the peak of Ottoman ceramic art. Produced in the town of Iznik from the late 15th century, these tiles and vessels achieved colors that European potters couldn't match for centuries. The famous 'Armenian bole' red—a thick, raised tomato-red that stands proud of the surface—remains difficult to replicate even today. Iznik potters painted tulips, carnations, hyacinths, and geometric arabesques on a crisp white ground. By the 17th century, the tradition had declined, and the exact recipes were lost.
story.reflection: What might be worth pursuing even if you can't fully achieve it?

image.alt: Iznik (Turkey; Iznik - Two Tiles - Google Art Project)

traditions.name: Oribe
traditions.visualCaption: Green and bold. The tea master's wild side.

story.hook: Named for a tea master executed for political intrigue, Oribe ware breaks every rule of Japanese restraint.
story.body: Furuta Oribe was a samurai, tea master, and student of Sen no Rikyū. Where Rikyū preferred austere black Raku bowls, Oribe embraced the unexpected: warped shapes, bold patterns, striking copper-green glazes splashed asymmetrically across the surface. The shapes seem almost to mock perfection—intentionally distorted, aggressively irregular. Oribe fell from political favor and was ordered to commit ritual suicide in 1615, but his aesthetic survived.
story.reflection: What rules might be worth breaking?

traditions.name: Pueblo Pottery
traditions.visualCaption: Earth, rain, and ancestors. The living tradition.

story.hook: In the American Southwest, pottery has been made continuously for over a thousand years—and it's still evolving.
story.body: Pueblo pottery traditions stretch back to the Ancestral Puebloans who built cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde and Chaco Canyon. Each Pueblo developed distinctive styles: the black-on-black of San Ildefonso, the polychrome of Acoma and Zuni, the micaceous clay of Taos, the carved redware of Santa Clara. The pottery is made without wheels, built by coiling and scraping, often fired outdoors using traditional fuels. Maria Martinez of San Ildefonso revived and transformed the black-on-black technique. Today, Pueblo potters navigate between honoring ancestral techniques and pushing into contemporary expression.
story.reflection: How does tradition enable rather than constrain creativity?

image.credit: Peter D. Tillman from USA / Wikimedia Commons

links.label: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

traditions.name: Song Dynasty Ceramics
traditions.visualCaption: The peak. Simplicity elevated to perfection.

story.hook: Many consider Song dynasty ceramics the greatest ever made—not for decoration, but for its absence.
story.body: The Song dynasty produced ceramics of such refined simplicity that collectors and potters have been trying to match them for 800 years. The famous 'five great kilns'—Ru, Guan, Ge, Jun, and Ding—each developed distinctive glazes and forms. Ru ware survives in fewer than 100 pieces; a single bowl can sell for tens of millions of dollars. What makes Song ceramics extraordinary isn't complexity but restraint. Forms are pure, often simple bowls and dishes. Glazes are usually monochrome—subtle celadons, creamy whites, lavender-streaked jun.
story.reflection: What would it mean to pursue simplicity as the highest goal?

image.alt: Song Dynasty Ceramics (Dish (Pan) with Garden Landscape LACMA M.73.48.106)

traditions.name: Joseon White Porcelain
traditions.visualCaption: Pure white. Confucian virtue made visible.

story.hook: While buncheong celebrated freedom, white porcelain embodied restraint—and became Korea's defining ceramic tradition.
story.body: Joseon white porcelain represents Neo-Confucian ideals made tangible: purity, simplicity, moral rectitude. After buncheong fell out of favor, white porcelain dominated Korean ceramics for four centuries. The finest pieces achieve an almost impossible purity—the white of fresh snow, the white of rice, the white of virtue itself. Moon jars (dalhanari) with their full-bellied embrace became iconic forms. The restraint can seem austere, but prolonged attention reveals endless subtlety.
story.reflection: What might restraint reveal that decoration would hide?

image.alt: Joseon White Porcelain (Joseon white porcelain plate, Korea)

traditions.name: Bizen
traditions.visualCaption: No glaze. Just earth and fire, arguing for weeks.

story.hook: Bizen potters fire their kilns for two weeks straight—then wait to see what the fire decided.
story.body: Bizen is the purest expression of wood-firing: no glaze, no decoration, just clay and fire. One of Japan's Six Ancient Kilns, Bizen has produced unglazed stoneware since the Kamakura period. Bizen's magic is in the kiln effects: hidasuki (red lightning-bolt patterns from straw), goma (sesame-seed spots where ash landed), sangiri (gray effects from pieces buried in embers). Each firing takes two weeks of continuous stoking, burning 10-15 tons of pine.
story.reflection: How long would you fire a kiln if you trusted the process?

image.alt: Bizen (Flower Vase called 'Tabimakura' (Portable pillow), Bizen ware, Edo period, 17th century - )

traditions.name: Yixing
traditions.visualCaption: Purple clay teapots. Where tea becomes ritual.

story.hook: The world's most famous teapots are never glazed—because the clay itself is the point.
story.body: Yixing has been producing stoneware teapots from local zisha ('purple sand') clay since the Ming dynasty. The clay is remarkable: dense, fine-grained, and naturally porous in ways that enhance the tea-brewing experience. A Yixing pot seasons over time, absorbing tea oils until it can almost brew tea without leaves. Traditionally, each pot is dedicated to a single type of tea. Master potters' work commands enormous prices; the forms are copied but never quite matched.
story.reflection: What object in your life has been seasoned by years of use?

traditions.name: Hagi
traditions.visualCaption: Soft, warm, alive. The tea bowl that ages with you.

story.hook: Tea masters say 'First Raku, second Hagi, third Karatsu'—and Hagi's soft surfaces change with every use.
story.body: Hagi ware began when Korean potters, brought to Japan after the invasions of the 1590s, settled in the domain of the Mōri clan. Hagi's distinctive character comes from its soft, porous body and its thick, crawling glazes in pale pink, cream, and white. The ware is famous for 'the seven changes of Hagi': the way pieces transform with use as tea stains penetrate the crackled glaze. A new Hagi bowl can seem bland, even chalky. A well-used one glows with decades of tea.
story.reflection: What in your life becomes more beautiful with use and age?

image.alt: Hagi (Hagi Ido teskål - chawan. Tamamura Shogetsu)

traditions.name: Karatsu
traditions.visualCaption: Korean roots, Japanese branches. Earthy, honest, warm.

story.hook: When Korean potters were brought to Kyushu, they created a tradition that became quintessentially Japanese.
story.body: Karatsu ware emerged in northern Kyushu, close to Korea, and shows its Korean heritage clearly: buncheong-influenced brushwork, slip decoration, climbing kilns. 'First Raku, second Hagi, third Karatsu' goes the tea ceremony ranking. The ware is earthy, often grayish-brown, with painted iron-brown decoration of simple grasses, birds, or abstract patterns. E-Karatsu (painted Karatsu) features bold brushwork; Madara-Karatsu (spotted Karatsu) shows rice-straw ash creating white patches.
story.reflection: How do traditions transform when they travel?

traditions.name: Imari / Arita
traditions.visualCaption: Export porcelain. Japan meets European desire.

story.hook: When Dutch traders needed porcelain and China was in chaos, Japanese potters filled the gap—and changed decorative arts forever.
story.body: In the early 17th century, Korean potters brought to Japan discovered porcelain stone near Arita in Kyushu. When Chinese exports collapsed during the Ming-Qing transition, Dutch traders turned to Arita to fill European demand. The result was 'Imari': boldly decorated porcelain featuring underglaze blue, overglaze red enamel, and gilding. European aristocrats couldn't get enough. The 'Kakiemon' style—delicate, asymmetrical, with ample white space—became particularly prized.
story.reflection: How does demand shape what makers create?

image.alt: Imari / Arita (Bowl 2, Imari ware, Edo period, 17th-18th century, stormy seascape design in overglaze ena)

traditions.name: Meissen
traditions.visualCaption: Europe's porcelain secret. White gold unlocked.

story.hook: An alchemist searching for gold accidentally discovered how to make porcelain—and ended China's monopoly forever.
story.body: For centuries, Europeans desperately wanted to make true hard-paste porcelain like the Chinese. Then in 1708, Johann Friedrich Böttger, an alchemist imprisoned by Augustus the Strong of Saxony to produce gold, instead discovered how to make porcelain using local kaolin clay. The Meissen factory was established in 1710, Europe's first hard-paste porcelain manufacturer. Its crossed-swords mark became a guarantee of quality. The secret eventually leaked—workers were bribed, techniques stolen—and porcelain factories spread across Europe.
story.reflection: What might you discover while searching for something else?

traditions.name: Staffordshire Pottery
traditions.visualCaption: Industry and art. Where the ceramic revolution began.

story.hook: In the hills of central England, a region transformed from craft workshops to the world's ceramic factory.
story.body: Staffordshire became England's ceramic heartland for practical reasons: local clay, local coal for firing, and access to canal transport. By the 18th century, the region's 'Five Towns' hosted hundreds of potteries. Josiah Wedgwood revolutionized production there, applying scientific method to ceramics, developing jasperware, and pioneering industrial techniques. Staffordshire produced everything: slip-decorated folk pottery, fine porcelain, transfer-printed wares that brought decorated ceramics to ordinary households.
story.reflection: How do we balance efficiency with handcraft?

traditions.name: Talavera
traditions.visualCaption: Spanish roots, Mexican flowers. Blue on white, forever.

story.hook: Spanish potters brought majolica techniques to Mexico—and indigenous artists transformed them into something new.
story.body: When Spanish colonizers arrived in Puebla, Mexico, they brought the tin-glazed majolica tradition from Talavera de la Reina in Spain. Indigenous potters, with their own rich ceramic heritage, learned and adapted the techniques. The result was Talavera Poblana: Spanish forms and techniques infused with Mexican colors, motifs, and spirit. Traditional Talavera uses only six colors on a creamy white base, painted freehand in intricate patterns. Every piece is made by hand.
story.reflection: What emerges when two traditions truly merge?

links.label: Artisanal Talavera of Puebla and Tlaxcala (Wikipedia)

traditions.name: Nok Terracotta
traditions.visualCaption: Africa's oldest known sculpture. Haunting, powerful, mysterious.

story.hook: In the 1940s, tin miners in Nigeria began finding ancient terracotta heads—and uncovered a civilization lost for 2,000 years.
story.body: The Nok culture produced Sub-Saharan Africa's oldest known figurative sculpture. These terracotta heads and figures, dating from 500 BCE to 200 CE, show remarkable sophistication: stylized features, elaborate hairstyles, detailed jewelry. The eyes are distinctive—triangular or semicircular, pierced through. We know almost nothing about the people who made them. Nok terracottas remind us how much African artistic history remains unknown.
story.reflection: What artistic traditions have been lost or remain undiscovered?

image.credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist / Wikimedia Commons

traditions.name: Zulu Pottery
traditions.visualCaption: Beer pots and beauty. Form follows ritual.

story.hook: In Zulu tradition, the shape of a pot reflects its purpose—and pottery-making belongs to women.
story.body: Zulu pottery is inseparable from Zulu life. Ukhamba (beer pots) for brewing traditional sorghum beer. Izinkamba for storing water. Each form optimized for its function. The pots are made by women, using techniques passed from mothers to daughters. No wheel—just coiling and smoothing by hand. The surfaces are burnished with smooth stones, then often blackened with smoke or graphite. Contemporary artists like Nesta Nala have brought Zulu pottery to international attention.
story.reflection: How does function shape form in your work?

image.alt: Zulu Pottery (Black pot Ukhamba Zulu people South Africa 17022019 4883)

traditions.name: Ancient Greek Pottery
traditions.visualCaption: Black and red. Stories painted in clay.

story.hook: On Greek vases, we can read mythology, watch athletes compete, and see daily life from 2,500 years ago.
story.body: Ancient Greek pottery is our window into the ancient world. The black-figure technique (black silhouettes on red clay, details incised) gave way to red-figure (red figures reserved against black, details painted in). Both techniques used the same iron-rich Attic clay, manipulated through oxidation and reduction firing. The scenes depicted everything: gods and heroes, symposia and athletics. Greek pottery influenced Roman ceramics and, rediscovered during the Renaissance, shaped European ideas about classical beauty.
story.reflection: What stories would you tell on a vessel?

traditions.name: Islamic Lusterware
traditions.visualCaption: Gold without gold. Light captured in glaze.

story.hook: Islamic potters invented a technique to make ceramics shimmer like metal—without using precious metals.
story.body: Lusterware is one of the great innovations in ceramic history. Developed in 9th-century Iraq, the technique deposits thin metallic films on the glaze surface, creating an iridescent sheen that shifts from gold to copper to ruby as the light changes. The process is demanding: painting metallic oxides onto an already-fired glazed surface, then re-firing in heavy reduction. The technique spread across the Islamic world and eventually to Italy.
story.reflection: What effect might be worth mastering despite its difficulty?

traditions.name: Tang Sancai
traditions.visualCaption: Three colors for the afterlife. Green, amber, white.

story.hook: The Tang dynasty's most distinctive ceramics were made for the dead—and never meant to be seen again.
story.body: Sancai means 'three colors,' though Tang potters often used more: amber, green, cream, sometimes blue. These lead-glazed earthenware pieces—horses, camels, guardian figures, vessels—were made as mingqi, burial goods for the wealthy dead. They weren't meant to be used or displayed; they accompanied the deceased into the tomb. When tombs were excavated in the 20th century, sancai became highly collectible—objects made for eternity, finally seen after a thousand years in darkness.
story.reflection: What would you make if no one would ever see it?

image.alt: Tang Sancai (唐 三彩碗-Bowl MET DP342650)

artists.name: Shoji Hamada
artists.visualCaption: The living national treasure who refused to sign his work.

story.hook: He was one of the most famous potters in the world—and he never signed a single pot.
story.body: Shoji Hamada was designated a 'Living National Treasure' by Japan in 1955. But Hamada rejected the idea of the artist-as-genius. Influenced by Yanagi Sōetsu's mingei philosophy, he believed true beauty emerged from anonymous craftsmanship. So he never signed his work. He settled in Mashiko, a humble pottery village, and spent his life making functional ware. His signature style—bold brush decoration, earthy ash glazes, confident form—emerged from thousands of repeated gestures.
story.reflection: What would your work look like if you stopped signing it?

image.credit: Unidentified (Ensian published by University of Michigan) / Wikimedia Commons

artists.name: Bernard Leach
artists.visualCaption: East meets West. The bridge builder.

story.hook: A British artist went to Japan to teach etching and discovered his life's purpose in a raku kiln.
story.body: Bernard Leach was 22, teaching in Tokyo, when a friend invited him to a raku party. Reaching into the hot kiln to pull out his still-glowing bowl, Leach felt something shift. He spent eleven years studying Japanese and Korean ceramics. When he returned to England in 1920 with Shoji Hamada, they established the Leach Pottery in St Ives. His book 'A Potter's Book' (1940) became the bible for generations of studio potters.
story.reflection: What traditions might you bridge?

links.label: A Potter's Book, Bernard Leach (Open Library)

artists.name: Lucie Rie
artists.visualCaption: Thin walls holding light. Volcanic surfaces.

story.hook: She fled the Nazis with nothing but her potter's wheel—and reinvented modern ceramics.
story.body: Lucie Rie was already an established potter in Vienna when the Nazis annexed Austria in 1938. She escaped to London with her wheel and little else. For years she made ceramic buttons to survive. Then Hans Coper arrived at her studio, and everything changed. Rie's work is recognizable instantly: impossibly thin walls, delicate feet, sophisticated forms that seem to hold light. Her volcanic glazes emerged from decades of experimentation. She worked until she was nearly 90.
story.reflection: What could you refine over a lifetime of practice?

image.alt: Lucie Rie (Bowl by Lucie Rie, National Museum Cardiff)

artists.name: Hans Coper
artists.visualCaption: Cycladic echoes. Ancient forms made new.

story.hook: A refugee who never trained as a potter created forms that seem to come from an ancient civilization that never existed.
story.body: Hans Coper fled Nazi Germany in 1939. In 1946, he answered an advertisement to assist Lucie Rie in her button-making business. He had no ceramic training, but within years, he was creating work unlike anything in ceramic history. His pieces evoke ancient Mediterranean pottery, Cycladic figures, African sculpture—yet they belong to no tradition. His 'spade forms,' 'thistle forms,' and composite vessels seem archaeological, as if excavated from a culture that existed only in his imagination.
story.reflection: What forms might you create that belong to no tradition?

image.alt: Hans Coper (Thrown Bottle by Hans Coper (YORYM-2004.1.807))

artists.name: Peter Voulkos
artists.visualCaption: Breaking the pot. Breaking the rules.

story.hook: He was a master thrower who decided to tear, slash, and stack his pots—and changed what ceramics could be.
story.body: Peter Voulkos could throw a perfect pot. Then, in the mid-1950s, influenced by Abstract Expressionism, he started doing violence to his work. He slashed thrown forms, stacked them, tore them open. The ceramic establishment was horrified. At Otis Art Institute in Los Angeles, he created a revolutionary program. His mature work—massive plates gouged with gestural marks, towering stacks of torn forms—proved that clay could carry the same emotional weight as any medium.
story.reflection: What rules might be worth breaking?

artists.name: Magdalene Odundo
artists.visualCaption: Body as vessel. Burnished to perfection.

story.hook: She studied pottery around the world—then created forms that seemed to exist outside time.
story.body: Magdalene Odundo was born in Kenya, trained in England, and studied traditional techniques in Nigeria, Kenya, and New Mexico. She absorbed it all—then synthesized something entirely her own. Her vessels are human: they have shoulders, necks, bellies, hips. Built by coiling, burnished with smooth stones, fired in sawdust, they carry the memory of African traditions while belonging to no single culture. Each piece takes weeks to complete.
story.reflection: What traditions might you synthesize into something new?

image.alt: Magdalene Odundo (Thrown, Burnished, Reduction Fired pot by Magdalene Odundo (YORYM-2004.1.950))

artists.name: Andile Dyalvane
artists.visualCaption: Xhosa traditions. Monumental scale.

story.hook: He grew up making clay oxen by the river—now his work fills museums on four continents.
story.body: Andile Dyalvane learned to work clay as a child in rural Eastern Cape, South Africa. Today his monumental vessels—scarified with marks that reference Xhosa body decoration and spiritual practices—command spaces in the Metropolitan Museum, the Denver Art Museum, and galleries worldwide. He co-founded Imiso Ceramics in Cape Town. Each piece carries Xhosa words and concepts: uBuhle (beauty), iThongo (ancestors), iLobola (bride wealth).
story.reflection: What knowledge from your childhood might transform your work?

artists.name: Edmund de Waal
artists.visualCaption: Porcelain and silence. Objects holding memory.

story.hook: He makes thousands of small white pots—and arranges them to hold the weight of history.
story.body: Edmund de Waal throws small porcelain vessels and arranges them in installations that fill vitrines, line walls, occupy entire rooms. The pots themselves are quiet, almost self-effacing. But in accumulation, they become powerful. His memoir 'The Hare with Amber Eyes' traces his family's history through a collection of Japanese netsuke. His installations often respond to specific sites, placing contemporary vessels in dialogue with centuries of collected things.
story.reflection: How might your pots carry memory?

image.alt: Edmund de Waal (Edmund de Waal with his installation, breathturn (2013), at Gagosian, New York (cropped))

links.label: The White Road, Edmund de Waal (Open Library)
The Hare with Amber Eyes, Edmund de Waal (Open Library)

artists.name: Yanagi Sōetsu
artists.visualCaption: The philosopher who saw beauty where others saw only utility.

story.hook: He wasn't a potter—but his ideas changed pottery forever.
story.body: Yanagi Sōetsu was a philosopher, art critic, and founder of the mingei (folk craft) movement. In the 1920s, while studying Korean Yi dynasty ceramics, he developed his theory: that true beauty emerged not from individual artistic genius but from the anonymous, unselfconscious work of traditional craftspeople. He gathered potters Shoji Hamada, Kanjiro Kawai, and Bernard Leach. Together they established the Japan Folk Crafts Museum and spread mingei philosophy worldwide.
story.reflection: What might you achieve by getting yourself out of the way?

image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author / Wikimedia Commons

links.label: The Unknown Craftsman, Soetsu Yanagi (Open Library)

artists.name: Kawai Kanjirō
artists.visualCaption: The mingei master who kept evolving.

story.hook: He was a technical perfectionist who abandoned perfection to find something more important.
story.body: Kawai Kanjirō began as a technically brilliant potter, mastering Chinese glazes. Then he met Yanagi Sōetsu and had a creative crisis. He destroyed much of his earlier work and committed to mingei philosophy. But unlike Hamada, Kawai kept evolving—from functional pottery to sculptural work, from traditional forms to wild experimentation. His home in Kyoto, now a museum, reveals a restless creative intelligence.
story.reflection: How might your work continue to evolve?

image.alt: Kawai Kanjirō (Kawai Kanjirō photographed by Shigeru Tamura)

artists.name: Maria Martinez
artists.visualCaption: Black-on-black. Tradition and innovation in one gesture.

story.hook: She revived an ancient technique, invented something new, and became the most famous Native American potter in history.
story.body: Maria Martinez was making traditional polychrome ware when archaeologists found ancient black pottery sherds. Working with her husband Julian, she rediscovered the reduction firing method. Then Julian invented something new: using guaco (wild plant juice) to paint matte designs on the burnished surface. The result—matte black on shiny black—became Maria's signature and made her internationally famous. In her later years, she signed her work collectively to spread the benefits.
story.reflection: How might tradition and innovation work together?

image.alt: Maria Martinez (Maria Martinez, San Ildefonso pottery maker)

links.label: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

artists.name: George Ohr
artists.visualCaption: The Mad Potter of Biloxi. A century ahead of his time.

story.hook: He called himself the greatest potter who ever lived—and stored thousands of unsold pieces, waiting for the world to catch up.
story.body: George Ohr was weird. He had a two-foot-long mustache. He threw impossibly thin-walled pieces and then crumpled, folded, twisted them into bizarre forms. Critics were baffled. So Ohr stacked his unsold work in the attic and waited. 'When I am gone,' he said, 'my work will be praised, honored, and cherished.' He was right. Today his pieces command prices in the hundreds of thousands.
story.reflection: What would you make if you trusted that the future would understand?

image.credit: Robert Brooks/Ohr-O'Keefe Museum of Art / Wikimedia Commons

artists.name: Beatrice Wood
artists.visualCaption: The mama of Dada lived to 105—and never stopped glazing.

story.hook: She was a Dadaist, a friend of Marcel Duchamp, and she didn't start making pottery until she was 40—then continued for 60 more years.
story.body: Beatrice Wood led many lives. She scandalized her family by becoming an actress, befriended Marcel Duchamp, helped create the Society of Independent Artists exhibition. Then, in her late 30s, she took a ceramic class. She was hooked. Moving to Ojai, California, she spent six decades mastering luster glazes. She continued working into her 100s. When asked the secret of her longevity: 'Art books, chocolates, and young men.'
story.reflection: What might you start at 40 and do for 60 years?

image.credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist / Wikimedia Commons

links.label: Beatrice Wood Center for the Arts

artists.name: Michael Cardew
artists.visualCaption: From Cornwall to Africa. Stoneware across continents.

story.hook: Bernard Leach's first student spent most of his life in Africa, creating a pottery tradition from scratch.
story.body: Michael Cardew was one of Bernard Leach's first students at St Ives. But England felt constraining. In 1942, he moved to Ghana, then to the Abuja Pottery in Nigeria. Cardew wasn't interested in transplanting English traditions; he wanted to develop an African stoneware tradition using local materials. His book 'Pioneer Pottery' documents his experiments. Many contemporary African potters trace their training to Cardew's workshops.
story.reflection: What might you build in a place completely different from where you started?

image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author / Wikimedia Commons

links.label: A Pioneer Potter, Michael Cardew (Open Library)

artists.name: Warren MacKenzie
artists.visualCaption: The humble potter. Thousands of pots, ordinary prices.

story.hook: He studied with Leach and Hamada, became one of America's most respected potters—and kept his prices low so ordinary people could buy.
story.body: Warren MacKenzie studied with Bernard Leach, apprenticed with Hamada. He settled in Minnesota and spent six decades making functional stoneware. Even as his reputation grew, he kept prices accessible. A MacKenzie bowl might cost what you'd pay for a department store dish. 'I make pots for people to use,' he said. He made hundreds of thousands, scattered across the country in ordinary kitchens.
story.reflection: What would it mean to keep your work accessible?

image.alt: Warren MacKenzie (Warren Mackenzie in studio, February 2017)

artists.name: Ken Price
artists.visualCaption: Color and form. Where pottery becomes sculpture.

story.hook: He started as a student of Voulkos, then went somewhere entirely his own.
story.body: Ken Price was part of the revolutionary circle around Peter Voulkos. But while Voulkos went big and gestural, Price went small, intimate, and intensely colored. His mature work—biomorphic forms covered in layers of acrylic paint, sanded and polished—occupies a space between pottery, sculpture, and painting. The colors are extraordinary: hot pinks, acid greens. He spent years on each piece, building up dozens of paint layers.
story.reflection: What happens when you take ceramics somewhere entirely your own?

artists.name: Toshiko Takaezu
artists.visualCaption: Closed forms. What happens inside the vessel.

story.hook: She closed her pots—sealed them shut, with a small clay ball inside, so they would ring when moved.
story.body: Toshiko Takaezu was born in Hawaii, studied with Maija Grotell, and developed one of the most distinctive voices in American ceramics. Her signature: closing the top of her vessels, leaving just a small hole or sealing them entirely. Inside each piece, she placed a small clay ball that rattled when moved—the pot keeping a secret. 'When working with clay,' she wrote, 'I find myself in a state of meditation.'
story.reflection: What might a pot contain that isn't visible?

artists.name: Ruth Duckworth
artists.visualCaption: Scale as sculpture. Walls that breathe.

story.hook: A refugee from Nazi Germany became one of the great ceramic sculptors, working from intimate vessels to monumental murals.
story.body: Ruth Duckworth fled Germany in 1936, trained as a sculptor, came to clay in her late 30s. In 1964, she moved to Chicago, and her work expanded dramatically. She created massive ceramic murals—'Earth, Water, Sky' covers 2,000 square feet—as well as intimate porcelain forms. 'Clay,' she said, 'is the stuff of life. We come from it and we return to it.'
story.reflection: What would happen if you dramatically changed scale?

artists.name: Phil Rogers
artists.visualCaption: Welsh ash and fire. Local materials, global tradition.

story.hook: He made glazes from the ash of Welsh trees and fired in wood kilns he built himself.
story.body: Phil Rogers was deeply committed to local materials and wood firing. From his pottery in rural Wales, he created functional stoneware using glazes made from ash collected from local trees. He built and rebuilt wood kilns, chasing the natural effects of ash landing on pots during firing. He was also a prolific writer, sharing knowledge through books on ash glazes and salt glazing.
story.reflection: What materials from your own landscape might you work with?

artists.name: Lisa Hammond
artists.visualCaption: Soda and flame. Firing with conviction.

story.hook: She's spent decades mastering soda firing—and teaching others to do the same.
story.body: Lisa Hammond is one of Britain's most respected functional potters, known for her soda-fired stoneware and commitment to the craft community. Working from her Greenwich pottery, she produces robust, generous forms with surfaces animated by the soda-firing process. She has taught extensively, demystifying soda firing through workshops and writing. She's also been a strong advocate for ceramics as a profession.
story.reflection: What technique might you spend decades mastering?

artists.name: Clary Illian
artists.visualCaption: Pots for the everyday. Function as meditation.

story.hook: She studied with Leach, apprenticed with Hamada, then spent decades making functional pots in small-town Iowa.
story.body: Clary Illian studied at the Leach Pottery and apprenticed with Shoji Hamada in Mashiko. She could have built a career on that pedigree alone. Instead, she returned to America, settled in Ely, Iowa (population: 2,000), and spent five decades making functional stoneware. 'A pot can be a friend,' she writes, 'a daily companion that serves you coffee and receives the use in a graceful way.'
story.reflection: What might a lifetime of making useful objects teach?

links.label: A Potter's Workbook, Clary Illian (Open Library)

artists.name: Shozo Michikawa
artists.visualCaption: Natural ash, twisted and split. The kiln as collaborator.

story.hook: He fires for days, then splits his pots with a chisel—revealing the fire's work inside.
story.body: Shozo Michikawa creates vessels that are as much kiln-made as hand-made. Working in Seto, he fires in a wood kiln for up to a week, allowing natural ash to build on surfaces. Then, after firing, he takes a dramatic step: splitting the vessels with a chisel, opening them to reveal interior surfaces where ash accumulated. The results are primal, geological—forms that seem hewn from volcanic rock.
story.reflection: What might you reveal by breaking something open?

artists.name: Jennifer Lee
artists.visualCaption: Quiet color. Vessels of contemplation.

story.hook: She hand-builds vessels so subtle they seem to hold silence.
story.body: Jennifer Lee creates hand-built stoneware vessels of extraordinary quietness. Her forms are simple—rounded, ovoid, gently asymmetrical—built slowly from coils over many weeks. The surfaces: subtle colors achieved through natural oxides and long, slow firings. She returns again and again to similar forms, finding endless variation. Lee was the first woman to win the Loewe Craft Prize.
story.reflection: What could you find in extreme restraint?

artists.name: Gwyn Hanssen Pigott
artists.visualCaption: Still life in porcelain. Arrangements of light.

story.hook: She grouped simple vessels together—and turned pottery into poetry.
story.body: Gwyn Hanssen Pigott studied with Bernard Leach, mastered wheel-thrown functional pottery. Then, in her 60s, she began arranging groups of pots together on rectangular boards. These 'still life' groupings—assemblies of bottles, bowls, beakers—transformed her work from craft into something closer to painting or poetry. The arrangements suggest Morandi's still life paintings, Chinese scholar's rocks, Japanese flower arrangement.
story.reflection: What happens when objects are arranged together?

artists.name: Akira Satake
artists.visualCaption: Salt-fired surfaces. Function with soul.

story.hook: A Japanese potter working in the American South, making pots that bridge cultures.
story.body: Akira Satake was born in Japan, trained in traditional pottery, then moved to the mountains of North Carolina. His work bridges both worlds: Japanese aesthetic sensitivity combined with American energy, salt-fired surfaces that glow with atmospheric effects. He's become deeply connected to the Appalachian pottery community while maintaining his Japanese roots.
story.reflection: What might emerge when cultures meet in clay?

artists.name: Svend Bayer
artists.visualCaption: Big pots, long firings. Wood fire at scale.

story.hook: He throws the largest pots in Britain—and fires them for days in a massive wood kiln.
story.body: Svend Bayer is known for large-scale thrown forms fired in wood kilns he built himself. His pots can stand four feet tall, generous forms with surfaces transformed by wood ash and flame. Bayer trained with Michael Cardew, absorbing the British studio pottery tradition, then developed his own path: bigger, bolder, more ambitious.
story.reflection: What would it mean to work at a scale that challenges you?

image.alt: Svend Bayer (Svend Bayer stoneware vase, Walker Art Gallery)
image.credit: Reptonix free Creative Commons licensed photos / Wikimedia Commons

artists.name: Nesta Nala
artists.visualCaption: Zulu master. Traditional technique, contemporary vision.

story.hook: She took traditional Zulu pottery and gave it a contemporary voice.
story.body: Nesta Nala was a Zulu master potter from KwaZulu-Natal. She learned traditional techniques from her mother and grandmother—coiling, burnishing, pit-firing—and then pushed them further than anyone had before. Her vessels grew larger, her surfaces more refined. The techniques were ancient; the vision was contemporary. She taught extensively, passing techniques to younger generations.
story.reflection: How can traditional techniques serve contemporary vision?

artists.name: Rosanjin
artists.visualCaption: Calligrapher, chef, potter. The aesthete who made dishes for his own food.

story.hook: He was a renowned calligrapher and restaurateur who made pottery so his food would look better.
story.body: Kitaōji Rosanjin defies categories. He was born into poverty, became famous as a calligrapher, opened exclusive restaurants, and became one of Japan's most distinctive potters. Rosanjin believed food, vessels, and environment formed an inseparable whole. He made pottery for his restaurants—plates designed to complement his cooking. His ceramic work draws on Bizen, Oribe, Shino, Seto, Kutani.
story.reflection: What if the vessel and its contents were designed together?

artists.name: Theaster Gates
artists.visualCaption: Clay and community. Urban transformation through craft.

story.hook: He trained as a potter—then used that training to reimagine entire neighborhoods.
story.body: Theaster Gates is an artist, social practice pioneer, and urban planner. But he started as a potter, training with Michael Simon. He still makes pots, but his practice has expanded: buying abandoned buildings on Chicago's South Side, transforming them into cultural spaces. Clay runs through his work: pieces from salvaged bricks, community firing events. For Gates, making pots and remaking communities are related acts.
story.reflection: What might your craft practice hold beyond the objects themselves?

image.alt: Theaster Gates (Unleashing Entrepreneurial Innovation with Stanford University Theaster Gates)

artists.name: Maija Grotell
artists.visualCaption: The mother of American ceramics. Teacher of teachers.

story.hook: She trained a generation of American ceramicists at Cranbrook—and pioneered the large-scale vessel.
story.body: Maija Grotell left Finland for America in 1927 and eventually headed the ceramics department at Cranbrook Academy of Art, where she taught for 28 years. Her students read like a who's who of American ceramics: Toshiko Takaezu, Richard DeVore, Howard Kottler. She pioneered large thrown forms with experimental glazes, combining Scandinavian craft traditions with American scale.
story.reflection: What legacy might you leave through teaching?

artists.name: Peter Lane
artists.visualCaption: Porcelain and precision. Geometric purity.

story.hook: He brings mathematical precision to porcelain—creating forms of extraordinary refinement.
story.body: Peter Lane makes translucent porcelain vessels with geometric precision. His forms—bowls, bottles, lidded containers—feature carved, fluted, or faceted surfaces that catch and hold light. The technical demands are extreme: porcelain at its thinnest is unforgiving, and Lane's forms require perfect control. He's also written extensively about studio ceramics, documenting the field's history and techniques.
story.reflection: What might extreme precision reveal?

artists.name: Ewen Henderson
artists.visualCaption: Mixed media, raw energy. Ceramics as painting.

story.hook: He combined different clays, bone ash, and metal oxides into raw, painterly vessels.
story.body: Ewen Henderson worked with mixed ceramic media, combining different clays, bone ash, and metal oxides to create surfaces of extraordinary complexity. His vessels feel more like geological formations than pottery—craggy, textured, alive with embedded color. Henderson trained as a painter, and his ceramic work carries that painterly sensibility: surfaces built up like impasto, colors layered and broken.
story.reflection: What happens when you bring another discipline's sensibility to clay?

image.alt: Ewen Henderson (Pinched, Coiled pot by Ewen Henderson (YORYM-2004.1.1377))

artists.name: Sandy Brown
artists.visualCaption: Wild clay, wild spirit. Joy in making.

story.hook: She's spent decades advocating for the joy and freedom in ceramic making.
story.body: Sandy Brown trained with Takeichi Kawai in Japan and makes bold, energetic earthenware—decorated with slips, oxides, and a distinctive gestural freedom. She's also a teacher, writer, and advocate for approaching ceramics with spontaneity and joy. Her book 'Freedom in Clay' captures her philosophy: that pottery can be liberating, expressive, and deeply personal.
story.reflection: How might you bring more joy to your making?

artists.name: Ken Matsuzaki
artists.visualCaption: Mashiko tradition, contemporary vision.

story.hook: He carries forward the Mashiko tradition while pushing it into contemporary territory.
story.body: Ken Matsuzaki works in Mashiko, the pottery village that Shoji Hamada made famous. He's deeply rooted in Mashiko traditions—wood firing, ash glazes, functional forms—but his work is distinctly contemporary: bolder, larger, more experimental than traditional Mashiko ware. He fires multiple wood kilns, each producing different effects, and has become one of Japan's most respected contemporary potters.
story.reflection: How do you honor tradition while making it your own?

places.name: Mashiko
places.visualCaption: Hamada's village. 300 potteries strong.

image.alt: Mashiko (Taisho-Showa Period Ko-Mashiko Ware Mado-e Dobin Window Picture Teapot Brooklyn Museum)
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: A farming town north of Tokyo became a world capital of pottery because one man chose to live there.
story.body:
Mashiko made everyday kitchen ware for Edo, rough and practical, from a coarse local clay. In 1924 Shoji Hamada, back from working with Bernard Leach in St Ives, settled here because the clay and the potters were unpretentious. He built his workshop and a climbing kiln, used local glazes from rice-straw ash, persimmon-coloured iron and kaki, and made Mashiko the heart of the Mingei movement.

Today there are hundreds of studios and shops. Twice a year, in spring and autumn, the Mashiko pottery fair fills the streets, and Hamada's house and kiln are kept as a museum. After the 2011 earthquake broke most of the town's kilns, potters rebuilt them together.
story.reflection: What would it take for a place to hold your work the way Mashiko held Hamada's?

places.tryIt: Look for a single, humble local clay body and build a small family of glazes around it, as Mashiko did with its own stone and ash.

places.name: Jingdezhen
places.visualCaption: The porcelain capital. A thousand years of white gold.

story.hook: For a thousand years, the world's porcelain came from one city in Jiangxi.
story.body:
Jingdezhen had kaolin and porcelain stone in the hills, pine for the kilns and a river to ship the ware. By the Song dynasty its qingbai, a shadowy blue-white, was famous; under the Yuan and Ming it made the blue-and-white porcelain that went to Persia, Africa and Europe and changed taste everywhere. The imperial kilns ran here, and work was split into dozens of specialised hands: one person threw, another trimmed, another painted only the rims.

The city still lives on porcelain. Old factories have become studios, markets sell every tool and mould, and residencies such as The Pottery Workshop and the Sanbao studios bring artists from all over the world to work beside local craftspeople.
story.reflection: What changes when a whole city shares one material?

places.tryIt: A residency here is a real possibility for a working potter; even a short one teaches porcelain throwing and trimming at a speed and skill few studios can.

places.name: Oaxaca / San Bartolo Coyotepec
places.visualCaption: Black clay country. Where midnight comes from mud.

story.hook: In the valleys of Oaxaca, whole villages are known by the colour of their clay.
story.body:
San Bartolo Coyotepec makes barro negro, the black ware polished with quartz and smoked in the kiln. Santa María Atzompa is known for green-glazed pots and Teodora Blanco's figures. In San Marcos Tlapazola, Zapotec women shape red clay by hand without a wheel and fire it in open bonfires. Ocotlán is the home of the Aguilar sisters' painted figures.

Much of this knowledge passes from mother to daughter, and many of these villages still dig their own clay and fire with wood. Markets in Oaxaca City gather it all, but the real lessons are in the family workshops.
story.reflection: What does it mean for a village to be its clay?

places.tryIt: Look at how San Marcos Tlapazola potters build and burnish without a wheel; it maps closely onto pinch and coil work with a local red clay.

places.name: Grottaglie
places.visualCaption: Workshops carved from rock. Puglia's ceramic caves.

story.hook: On the heel of Italy, a quarter of the town is still given over to potteries carved into the rock.
story.body:
Grottaglie, in Puglia, has made ceramics since at least the Middle Ages. Its Quartiere delle Ceramiche is a street of workshops built into the soft tufa, with kilns and storerooms cut into the hillside. The town is known for capasoni, huge wine and oil jars, for pumi, the bud-shaped finials put on balconies for luck, and for glazed maiolica in green, blue and yellow.

A school, a ceramics museum in the Episcopio castle and a yearly competition keep the craft current, and many workshops still welcome visitors to watch.
story.reflection: What objects in your own town are made for luck?

places.tryIt: The pumo is a perfect small project: a closed, thrown bud form with a crown of leaves, made to stand on a wall.

places.name: St Ives / Leach Pottery
places.visualCaption: Where East met West. The birthplace of British studio pottery.

story.hook: A fishing town in Cornwall became the place where studio pottery in the West began.
story.body:
In 1920 Bernard Leach and Shoji Hamada set up a pottery on the edge of St Ives, built a Japanese-style climbing kiln and began making stoneware with local materials. Leach's A Potter's Book (1940) came out of this workshop and taught generations of potters to see a pot as both useful and expressive.

The Leach Pottery still runs as a working studio, museum and training pottery, with an apprenticeship-style programme. St Ives also became a painters' colony, with Barbara Hepworth's studio and the Tate St Ives a short walk away.
story.reflection: What would a workshop that trains as it makes look like for you?

places.tryIt: The Leach Pottery's standard ware is a good study in a small, repeated range; try making ten of one form and keeping only the best three.

places.name: Stoke-on-Trent
places.visualCaption: The Potteries. Where industry met art.

story.hook: The Potteries: six towns that industrialised ceramics and supplied the world's tables.
story.body:
From the 18th century Stoke-on-Trent had coal for kilns, clay nearby and canals to move it. Josiah Wedgwood, Spode, Minton and later Royal Doulton made it the centre of English pottery, inventing creamware, jasperware and bone china, and printing patterns that are still in use. At its peak the skyline was a forest of bottle ovens.

Most of the great factories have closed or shrunk, but the city has been reinventing itself: the Potteries Museum and Gladstone Pottery Museum keep the history, the British Ceramics Biennial brings new work, and makers are moving into the old works.
story.reflection: What is lost, and what is gained, when making moves from a hand to a factory?

places.tryIt: Visit or study the bottle ovens and the division of labour; the way a factory breaks a pot into steps is a useful lens on your own process.

places.name: Shigaraki Town
places.visualCaption: Six Ancient Kilns country. Fire marks and tanuki.

story.hook: One of Japan's six ancient kilns, where the clay itself carries the fire's colours.
story.body:
Shigaraki, near Lake Biwa, sits on a coarse clay full of feldspar grains. In long wood firings those grains burst and melt on the surface, the clay flashes orange and scarlet, and falling ash runs into green glass. Tea masters prized its unglazed jars from the 16th century on.

Today it is known for big tanuki statues outside every shop, but also for serious work: the Shigaraki Ceramic Cultural Park runs one of the world's best-known residencies, with large kilns and studio space for international artists.
story.reflection: How much of the finished pot do you leave to the fire?

places.tryIt: The Ceramic Cultural Park's artist-in-residence programme is worth applying to; it is open to international artists.

places.name: Arita
places.visualCaption: Japan's porcelain birthplace. Where Korean knowledge met Japanese ambition.

image.alt: Arita (Arita porcelain bottle, Edo period (1615-1868), Japan)

story.hook: Where Japan's porcelain began, with a Korean potter and a mountain of stone.
story.body:
Around 1616, Yi Sam-pyeong, one of the Korean potters brought to Japan after the invasions of the 1590s, is said to have found porcelain stone at Izumiyama near Arita. Within decades Arita was making blue-and-white and then brilliant enamelled porcelain. Shipped from the port of Imari, it filled European palaces when Chinese exports stopped in the mid-17th century.

The Kakiemon and Imaemon families still work there, the quarry can be visited, and each spring the Arita Ceramic Fair draws over a million people.
story.reflection: How does one discovery of a material reshape a whole region?

places.tryIt: Study Kakiemon's use of empty white space; it is a lesson in how little decoration a pot needs.

places.name: Vallauris
places.visualCaption: Picasso's pottery town. Mediterranean clay, modern art.

story.hook: A small town on the Riviera where Picasso came to play with clay.
story.body:
Vallauris had made cooking pots, the culinaire ware, since the Middle Ages. By the 1940s the trade was dying when Picasso visited the Madoura workshop of Suzanne and Georges Ramié in 1946. He returned and made thousands of pieces there over the next decades: plates, owls, vases turned into women.

His presence drew artists and revived the town. The Musée Magnelli and Musée de la Céramique hold collections, and the Madoura workshop and a biennial of contemporary ceramics keep the place a centre for clay.
story.reflection: What would you make if you met clay for the first time, as Picasso did here at 65?

places.tryIt: Take a set of thrown plates and treat each one as a canvas, as Picasso did: slips, wax resist and sgraffito on bisque.

places.name: Seto
places.visualCaption: Six Ancient Kilns. The town that gave ceramics its Japanese name.

image.alt: Seto (Wide-Mouthed Storage Jar with Peony Vines)

story.hook: A city so tied to pottery that its name became the Japanese word for ceramics.
story.body:
Seto, near Nagoya, has fired glazed stoneware since the 13th century, longer than any other Japanese centre, and setomono still means everyday ceramics in Japanese. Its clays and early ash and iron glazes imitated Chinese wares, then grew into their own: the yellow Seto, Shino and Oribe of the Momoyama period were made in the hills here and in nearby Mino.

The city has a large ceramics museum, a Novelty Museum of industrial figurines, and dozens of working kilns.
story.reflection: What everyday object would you want your name to mean?

places.tryIt: Compare yellow Seto and Shino: both come from local feldspar and clay, a good model for testing what your own local materials do.

places.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
places.visualCaption: Five thousand years under one roof.

image.alt: Metropolitan Museum of Art (Jar with Dragon - MET - Joy of Museums)

story.hook: Five thousand years of clay in one building on Fifth Avenue.
story.body:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art's ceramics run across almost every department: Chinese porcelain, Japanese tea wares, Greek vases, Islamic lustreware, European porcelain, American art pottery and studio ceramics. The Asian and Islamic galleries are the richest, and the online collection lets you zoom into thousands of pieces in detail.

Its Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, written by the curators, is one of the best free introductions to ceramic history anywhere.
story.reflection: Which single piece would you want to sit with for an hour?

places.tryIt: Use the Met's open-access images: pick one historical form a week and throw or build your own answer to it.

places.name: Victoria and Albert Museum
places.visualCaption: The world's greatest decorative arts collection.

story.hook: The largest ceramics collection in the world, in South Kensington.
story.body:
The V&A's ceramics galleries hold tens of thousands of pieces across a whole floor, from ancient Chinese wares to Iznik tiles, Delftware and contemporary studio pottery. There is a gallery of world ceramics arranged so you can compare techniques side by side, and a study room with drawers to open.

The museum has a ceramics studio for residencies and demonstrations, and its collection is searchable online.
story.reflection: What happens when you see a thousand years of one technique in one room?

places.tryIt: Look at the study galleries by technique, for example tin glaze across Spain, Italy and the Netherlands, and note how the same idea changes by place.

places.name: Faenza
places.visualCaption: Where 'faience' got its name. Italian majolica's heart.

image.alt: Faenza (Faenza maiolica, piatto con leandro, 1525 ca.)

story.hook: The town that gave its name to faience.
story.body:
Faenza, in Emilia-Romagna, was one of the great centres of Renaissance maiolica: tin-glazed earthenware painted in bright colours. Its white-ground bianchi di Faenza were so admired that French speakers called all such ware faïence.

The International Museum of Ceramics (MIC) holds one of the world's largest collections, and the Premio Faenza, one of the oldest international ceramics competitions, has run since 1938. The town is still full of workshops and an art school dedicated to ceramics.
story.reflection: What would your work look like on a pure white ground?

places.tryIt: The Premio Faenza is open internationally; watch for its next call.

places.name: Fez
places.visualCaption: Blue tiles, blue sky. Morocco's ceramic soul.

image.alt: Fez (Bab Bou Jeloud Frame Minaret Fes Nov25 A7CR 09127-8 HDR3)
image.credit: This Photo was taken by Timothy A. Gonsalves . Feel free to use my pho / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: Blue-and-white bowls and mosaic tiles cut by hand in an ancient medina.
story.body:
Fez has made pottery for over a thousand years. Its famous cobalt-blue painted ware and its zellige, mosaic tiles cut piece by piece from glazed squares and set into geometric patterns, decorate mosques, fountains and houses across Morocco.

In the potters' quarter outside the old walls, workshops still dig and mix clay, throw, glaze and fire in wood and gas kilns, and the zellige cutters work with a hammer on a stone.
story.reflection: How does a pattern change when every piece is cut by hand?

places.tryIt: Zellige is a lesson in geometry: try a small panel of hand-cut glazed tiles built from one simple star pattern.

places.name: Seagrove
places.visualCaption: America's pottery capital. Where traditions run deep.

story.hook: A crossroads in North Carolina with over a hundred potteries along its roads.
story.body:
Seagrove sits on rich local clay, and potters have worked there since the 18th century, making salt-glazed jugs and churns for farm families. When that trade faded, families like the Owens, Cole and Teague kept going by selling to tourists and collectors, and a new generation arrived from the 1970s on.

Today it is the largest community of working potters in the US, many with wood and salt kilns, and the North Carolina Pottery Center explains its history.
story.reflection: What keeps a craft alive when its first use disappears?

places.tryIt: Salt and wood firing are still everyday practice here; a visit or workshop is one of the best ways to learn them in the US.

places.name: Icheon
places.visualCaption: Korea's living ceramic heritage. Celadon revived.

story.hook: Korea's ceramic city, where the celadon and buncheong of the past are made again.
story.body:
Icheon, south-east of Seoul, has good clay and became a centre for reviving Korean celadon, white porcelain and buncheong in the 20th century, after these traditions had nearly disappeared. Today hundreds of kilns work here, from master potters to small studios, and the Icheon Ceramic Festival draws large crowds.

The Korea Ceramic Foundation runs the Icheon World Ceramic Center and organises the Korean International Ceramic Biennale, one of the major international ceramics events.
story.reflection: What does it take to bring a lost tradition back?

places.tryIt: Buncheong's white slip over grey clay is easy to try with commercial bodies: brush, dip or inlay a white slip and carve through it.

places.name: La Borne
places.visualCaption: French wood-fire heartland. Salt and ash.

story.hook: A tiny village in the Berry where wood-fired stoneware never stopped.
story.body:
La Borne, in central France, made salt- and wood-fired stoneware for centuries from local clay. After the Second World War, artists such as Jean and Jacqueline Lerat and Vassil Ivanoff settled here and turned it into a centre of modern French ceramics.

Around seventy potters now work in and around the village, many with wood kilns, including anagama and noborigama. A contemporary ceramics centre shows their work, and firings are often open to visitors.
story.reflection: What does it mean to choose a village because of its kilns?

places.tryIt: The village holds open firings; it is a good place to see a large wood kiln loaded and fired.

places.name: Tokoname
places.visualCaption: Six Ancient Kilns. Red clay, drainage pipes, and tea.

image.alt: Tokoname (Jar, Tokoname ware, Heian period, 12th century, excavated at Mizoguchi, Futami-cho, Ise-sh)

story.hook: Another of Japan's six ancient kilns, famous for its red teapots and its kiln chimneys.
story.body:
Tokoname, south of Nagoya, has made pottery since the 12th century. It produced huge storage jars for centuries, then drainpipes and tiles in the industrial age, and is best known now for its small red-clay teapots with side handles, the kyusu, made from an iron-rich local clay that is often left unglazed.

The Pottery Footpath winds between old kilns, brick chimneys and walls built from broken pipes and saggars. The town is also home to the INAX Live Museum of tiles and terracotta.
story.reflection: What can a single, perfectly made small form teach?

places.tryIt: The kyusu is a hard and rewarding exercise: a lid that fits, a strainer and a side handle that balances in the hand.

places.name: Deruta
places.visualCaption: Umbrian majolica. Renaissance patterns still painted by hand.

image.alt: Deruta (Dish with a Peacock Feather Pattern)
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: A hill town in Umbria known for painted maiolica and gold lustre.
story.body:
Deruta has made tin-glazed maiolica since at least the 14th century. In the Renaissance its workshops became famous for lustre, an iridescent metallic shine fired in reduction, and for large display plates painted with portraits and stories.

Today dozens of family workshops paint traditional patterns by hand, and the Regional Ceramics Museum holds over six thousand pieces.
story.reflection: What story would you paint on a single large plate?

places.tryIt: Maiolica painting on an unfired tin glaze is approachable with a commercial majolica glaze and stains; it rewards a confident brush.

places.name: Kyoto
places.visualCaption: Tea ceremony capital. Where Raku was born.

story.hook: The old capital, where pottery was made for the tea ceremony and the court.
story.body:
Kyoto's potters, working near the temples and the court, made refined wares known as Kyo-yaki and Kiyomizu-yaki, with painted enamels developed by Nonomura Ninsei and Ogata Kenzan in the 17th and early 18th centuries. It is also where the Raku family has made tea bowls for over four hundred years, and where Kawai Kanjiro, a founder of the Mingei movement, had his house and kiln.

The Kawai Kanjiro Memorial House and the Raku Museum can both be visited, and the Gojozaka pottery fair fills the streets each August.
story.reflection: How does making for a ritual change the way you make?

places.tryIt: Spend time with Kenzan's square dishes, where painting and form are one design; try a slab dish painted as a single image.

surfaces.name: Volcanic

story.hook: A surface that looks as if it boiled and froze in the moment of cooling.
story.body:
Volcanic or crater glazes trap gas as they melt. Silicon carbide added to a glaze gives off gas in the firing and leaves bubbles and craters; very high-calcium or underfired glazes can blister on their own. Thick application and a fast cool freeze the bubbles in place.

The result is pitted, lunar and tactile: beautiful on sculpture and planters, poor on anything that touches food or lips, because the craters hold dirt and can be sharp.
story.reflection: When does a 'fault' become the whole point?

surfaces.tryIt: Add about 1 to 2 percent silicon carbide to a glaze you know and fire a test tile thick and thin; keep it for outsides and sculptural work.

surfaces.name: Liquid

story.hook: Glaze that still looks wet, pooled in the bottom of a bowl like water.
story.body:
A liquid look comes from a glossy, fluid glaze that runs to the low points and gathers there in a deep, clear pool, often thicker and darker in colour where it collects. Celadons and clear glazes over textured or carved surfaces show it best, and so do ash glazes that run in the kiln.

The trade-off is movement: fluid glazes can run off the pot, so they are applied thinner on the lower walls and fired on a cookie or with a wide unglazed foot.
story.reflection: Where on a pot would you want light to collect?

surfaces.tryIt: Pour a little extra glaze into the bottom of a bowl before firing and see how a pool forms; leave a generous bare foot.

surfaces.name: Stone

image.alt: Stone (Teapot in the shape of a sheng, Yixing, China, unglazed brown stoneware - Victoria and Alb)

story.hook: Clay that, when it comes out of the kiln, looks and feels like rock.
story.body:
Stony surfaces come from matte, dry glazes, often high in alumina or magnesia, or from leaving the clay bare and letting the fire mark it. Grogged or sandy bodies, slips with granite dust, and reduction firing add the speckle and depth of real stone.

This is the territory of Shigaraki jars, of stoneware's very name, and of many contemporary potters who want their pots to look found rather than made.
story.reflection: What would it mean for your pot to look as if it had always existed?

surfaces.tryIt: Wedge a little coarse grog or sieved local sand into a commercial stoneware and leave the outside bare; compare it with a dolomite matte glaze.

surfaces.name: Skin

story.hook: Surfaces that invite the hand: soft, warm and almost alive.
story.body:
Skin-like surfaces are satin to matte, never shiny, and often warm in colour. They come from burnishing bare clay, from terra sigillata, from satin glazes that are just past melting, or from soda and wood firing that leaves a thin, uneven sheen.

They change with use: hands polish them, oils darken them, and a pot with a skin surface ages like leather.
story.reflection: How does a surface change how someone holds a pot?

surfaces.tryIt: Burnish a leather-hard pot with the back of a spoon, then fire it low; compare it with the same form in a satin glaze.

surfaces.name: Natural Ash
surfaces.visualCaption: Where the fire left its mark.

story.hook: Glaze made by fire itself, from the ash of the wood that fires the kiln.
story.body:
In a wood kiln, ash flies through the chamber and settles on the pots. At high temperature it melts with the clay surface into a glaze, usually green to amber, often running in drips down the side facing the fire. Potters learned to imitate it by mixing wood ash with clay and feldspar into a glaze.

Every ash is different: oak, pine, rice straw and fruitwood each give their own colour and melt, which is why ash glazes are a classic way of using local materials.
story.reflection: What would your glaze be if it came from your own fire?

surfaces.tryIt: A classic start: 40 percent wood ash, 40 percent feldspar, 20 percent clay. Wash and sieve the ash first, wear gloves, and test at cone 6 and cone 10.

surfaces.name: Crystalline

story.hook: Glazes that grow frost-like crystals while the kiln cools.
story.body:
Crystalline glazes are low in alumina and high in zinc, often with titanium. Held at a specific temperature during cooling, zinc silicate crystals grow outward from seeds into fans and flowers, sometimes several centimetres across.

They are runny and demanding: pots sit on catch basins, firing schedules are precise, and results vary from firing to firing, which is part of the fascination.
story.reflection: How much control do you want over the final image?

surfaces.tryIt: Crystalline needs a controller with programmable holds; ask a studio with a digital kiln if you can run a test with catchers.

surfaces.name: Shino

image.alt: Shino (Tea Bowl known as 'Furisode', Mino ware, Shino type, Azuchi-Momoyama to Edo period, 16th-1)

story.hook: Thick, white to orange, pitted and carbon-flecked: the first white glaze of Japan.
story.body:
Shino was developed in the Mino region in the late 16th century from local feldspar and a little clay, applied very thick. In a long, slow reduction firing it turns milky white with orange blushes where it is thin, and small pinholes and crawls where it shrinks. American potters in the 1970s developed carbon-trap Shinos with soda ash that trap grey and black carbon in the glaze.

It is a glaze about accident and depth, prized for tea bowls.
story.reflection: Do you want a glaze you control, or one that answers back?

surfaces.tryIt: Shino needs reduction at cone 10; it is worth asking which Bay Area studios fire gas reduction and whether they keep a Shino bucket.

surfaces.name: Tenmoku

image.credit: Anonymous ( Japan ) Unknown author / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: A deep iron glaze, black where thick and rust-brown where it breaks over an edge.
story.body:
Tenmoku comes from Chinese iron glazes of the Song dynasty, especially the Jian tea bowls of Fujian, which Japanese monks brought home from Mount Tianmu. It is a high-fire glaze with around 8 to 12 percent iron oxide that melts glossy black and breaks to rust where it is thin.

Variations include oil-spot and hare's fur, where iron crystallises on the surface. Modern cone 6 tenmokus make the look possible in an electric kiln.
story.reflection: What do edges show that flat surfaces hide?

surfaces.tryIt: Carve or throw rings into a form before glazing: a tenmoku breaks rust on every edge and shows the texture beautifully.

surfaces.name: Salt Glaze
surfaces.visualCaption: Fire and salt, married in the kiln.

image.alt: Salt Glaze (The Art of German Stoneware Philadelphia 2012 010)
image.credit: Picture taken by Marcus Cyron / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: Glaze made by throwing salt into a red-hot kiln.
story.body:
At about 1,250°C, salt thrown into the firebox turns to vapour, and the sodium reacts with silica in the clay to form a thin glaze on every exposed surface. The result has an orange-peel texture, a soft sheen and colour that depends on the clay and any slips beneath.

German potters developed salt glaze in the 15th century and it became the classic finish for jugs and crocks in Europe and America. It needs a dedicated kiln, because the salt glazes the kiln itself; soda firing is a related, less corrosive method.
story.reflection: What would it be like for the whole kiln to glaze your work?

surfaces.tryIt: Look for a soda or salt kiln community firing; many studios that have one let members put work in for a fee.

surfaces.name: Carbon Trap

story.hook: Grey and black smoke caught inside a glaze for good.
story.body:
Carbon trapping happens when a glaze containing soda ash or other soluble sodium melts early in a reduction firing, sealing carbon from the smoky atmosphere into the surface. It shows as grey shadows and black flecks, especially in Shino glazes.

It depends on timing: heavy reduction early, before the glaze seals, is what captures the carbon, which is why results vary across the kiln.
story.reflection: What marks of the making process would you like to keep visible?

surfaces.tryIt: This only happens in gas or wood reduction; ask at a cone 10 reduction studio to try a carbon-trap Shino with early body reduction.

surfaces.name: Oil Spot

story.hook: A black glaze scattered with silver spots, like drops of oil on water.
story.body:
Oil-spot comes from Song dynasty Jian ware. During firing, iron oxide releases oxygen and bubbles rise through the glaze, carrying iron to the surface where it crystallises as metallic spots on the black ground. The most prized example, the yohen tenmoku bowls in Japan, are national treasures.

It needs a high-iron, thick glaze and a carefully controlled firing; modern potters have made reliable versions at cone 10 and even cone 6.
story.reflection: What would you make if one bowl could hold a whole night sky?

surfaces.tryIt: Test a published cone 6 oil-spot recipe very thick on a tile; it is one of the more achievable 'special' glazes in an electric kiln.

surfaces.name: Crawling/Lichen
surfaces.visualCaption: When glaze gives up and becomes texture.

story.hook: Glaze that pulls back into islands, leaving the clay bare between them.
story.body:
Crawling happens when a glaze shrinks a lot as it dries or does not stick well to the surface, so it pulls apart in the firing and beads up. Usually it is a defect, caused by dusty bisque, thick application or high-shrinkage materials.

Some potters push it on purpose, with magnesium carbonate glazes that crack and crawl into lichen-like patterns.
story.reflection: What could a defect you fear become if you used it on purpose?

surfaces.tryIt: A lichen glaze (often with 20 percent or more magnesium carbonate) applied thick over a contrasting slip shows crawling at its best. Keep it off food surfaces.

surfaces.name: Celadon
