surfaces.visualCaption: Sky after rain. Jade made from fire.

image.alt: Celadon (Foliate Dish with Bovine (Xiniu) Gazing at a Crescent Moon)

story.hook: Jade-green glass, deepest where it pools.
story.body:
Celadon is a clear glaze with a little iron, about 1 to 2 percent, fired in reduction, so the iron turns blue-green. It was perfected in China from the Yue kilns to the Song Longquan wares, and in Korea during the Goryeo dynasty, where potters added inlaid slip decoration.

Because it is transparent, it darkens wherever it is thick, so carving and fluting under celadon read as shadows.
story.reflection: How would you carve a pot to give a glaze somewhere to pool?

surfaces.tryIt: Carve or flute a pot before bisque and glaze it in celadon; the carving turns into lines of deeper green.

surfaces.name: Copper Red
surfaces.visualCaption: Blood red from copper. Reduction's prize.

image.credit: Anonymous (Chinese artist) Unknown author / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: A red from copper and smoke: the hardest colour in the old kilns.
story.body:
Copper in a glaze is green in oxidation, but in heavy reduction it becomes tiny particles of metallic copper that read as deep red. Chinese potters of the Ming and Qing dynasties made sang de boeuf (oxblood) and the softer peach bloom reds, both hard to control.

Modern potters make copper reds in gas reduction, and cone 6 versions use a little silicon carbide in the glaze to reduce the copper locally even in an electric kiln.
story.reflection: What colours of yours depend on the atmosphere, not the recipe?

surfaces.tryIt: A cone 6 copper red with a pinch of silicon carbide is a classic test in an electric kiln; fire it on a vertical tile to see thick and thin.

surfaces.name: Hare's Fur

story.hook: Fine brown and gold streaks running through black glaze, like animal fur.
story.body:
Hare's fur is another Song dynasty Jian ware glaze: as an iron-saturated glaze runs down the pot, iron crystallises into fine streaks. Tea masters in China and Japan prized these bowls for whisked tea, which showed well against the dark glaze.

It needs a fluid, high-iron glaze applied thick on the upper part of the pot so it streaks as it runs.
story.reflection: What does movement during firing leave behind?

surfaces.tryIt: Apply a high-iron glaze thick at the rim and thin at the foot, and fire on a tile; the run is what makes the fur.

techniques.name: Coiling
techniques.visualCaption: The oldest way. Rope after rope of clay.

story.hook: The oldest way to build a pot: one rope of clay at a time.
story.body:
Coiling is found on every continent and in the oldest pottery we know, from Jōmon Japan to the great water jars of Africa and the Americas. Ropes of clay are laid in rings or spirals and joined by pinching and scraping, so a pot can grow larger and freer than on a wheel, and in any shape.

The walls can be smoothed with a rib until the coils vanish, or left visible as texture. Many potters work on a turntable, letting each few coils firm up before adding more.
story.reflection: What shapes become possible when there is no wheel turning them round?

techniques.tryIt: Build a tall form in stages over two or three days, letting each section reach soft leather-hard before you add the next.

techniques.name: Burnishing
techniques.visualCaption: Polish until the clay shines from within.

story.hook: Polishing raw clay with a stone until it shines without any glaze.
story.body:
Burnishing presses the fine clay particles flat so the surface reflects light. It is done at leather-hard with a smooth stone, a spoon or the back of a bone, often over a fine slip or terra sigillata. Potters from ancient Egypt to San Ildefonso Pueblo to Rwanda have used it to give bare clay a soft gloss.

The shine survives only low firings, around cone 010 to 06; higher temperatures dull it. It pairs naturally with pit, saggar and smoke firing.
story.reflection: What does a surface feel like when it was made only by hand and stone?

techniques.tryIt: Burnish a leather-hard pot, rest it, burnish again when bone-dry, and bisque low; then try a smoke or saggar firing.

techniques.name: Wood Firing
techniques.visualCaption: Days of fire. Tons of wood. Gifts from the kiln.

story.hook: Days of stoking, where flame and ash paint the pots.
story.body:
In a wood kiln the fire travels across the ware, leaving flashing, ash glaze and colour shifts that no electric kiln can make. Firings last from a day to over a week, with a crew stoking in shifts, and each pot carries a record of where it sat and how the fire moved past it.

Anagama, noborigama, train and catenary kilns all fire with wood. Many Bay Area and West Coast potters share wood kilns and fire together a few times a year.
story.reflection: What does it mean to make work with a group, around a fire?

techniques.tryIt: Join a community wood firing as a stoker; it is the best way to learn how loading and the fire's path shape the pots.

techniques.name: Sgraffito
techniques.visualCaption: Scratch through the surface. Reveal what's beneath.

story.hook: Scratching through a layer of slip to draw with the clay underneath.
story.body:
Sgraffito, from the Italian for 'scratched', means covering leather-hard clay with a contrasting slip and carving through it to reveal the body. It was used in Byzantine and Islamic pottery, in Italy and in English and German slipware, and is popular again for its graphic, drawn quality.

Timing matters: the slip should be dry to the touch but the clay still soft enough to carve cleanly.
story.reflection: What would you draw if your line had to cut into the pot?

techniques.tryIt: Brush black or dark slip on a leather-hard piece, wait until it loses its shine, and carve with a loop tool or sharpened stick.

techniques.name: Pit Firing
techniques.visualCaption: Fire in the earth. The original kiln.

image.credit: Marco Bellucci from Scandicci, Italy / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: Firing in a hole in the ground, with sawdust, leaves and dung.
story.body:
Pit firing is the earliest way of firing pottery and is still used in many parts of the world. Burnished pots are packed in a pit with combustibles: sawdust, wood, straw, seaweed, salts and metals such as copper carbonate. They are covered and left to burn, often overnight.

The low, smoky fire gives blacks, greys, reds and flashes of colour. Pots stay porous and are decorative rather than for food or water.
story.reflection: How do you feel about letting chance finish your work?

techniques.tryIt: Artillery Ceramics in the Mission runs seasonal pit firings; a good way to try it without digging a pit yourself.

techniques.name: Reduction Firing
techniques.visualCaption: Starve the fire of oxygen. Transform the chemistry.

story.hook: Starving the fire of oxygen to change the colour of clay and glaze.
story.body:
In a fuel-burning kiln, cutting the air supply makes the flame hunt for oxygen in the clay and glazes. Iron turns from brown to blue-green or black, copper turns red, and clay bodies darken and speckle. Celadon, Shino, tenmoku and copper red all depend on reduction.

Electric kilns fire in oxidation, so reduction means gas or wood kilns; some Bay Area studios run cone 10 gas reduction for members.
story.reflection: How much of a glaze's colour is the recipe, and how much is the air?

techniques.tryIt: Fire the same glaze in oxidation and in reduction and set the two tiles side by side; it is the best way to learn what reduction does.

techniques.name: Kintsugi
techniques.visualCaption: Broken, mended, more beautiful. Gold in the cracks.

image.alt: Kintsugi (Tea bowl, Korea, Joseon dynasty, 16th century AD, Mishima-hakeme type, buncheong ware, sto)

story.hook: Mending broken pots with lacquer and gold, so the break becomes part of the story.
story.body:
Kintsugi developed in Japan, traditionally dated to the 15th century, as a way of repairing precious tea wares with urushi lacquer dusted with powdered gold. Rather than hiding the break, it highlights it, in line with the appreciation of wear and age in wabi-sabi.

Traditional urushi is a skin irritant and takes weeks to cure in a humid box; simpler kits use epoxy and mica, but are not food safe.
story.reflection: Which of your broken pots deserve a second life?

techniques.tryIt: Keep the cracked pieces from a firing and practise on one; if you want food-safe results, look for a class in true urushi kintsugi.

techniques.name: Slip Trailing
techniques.visualCaption: Drawing with liquid clay. Lines that rise.

image.alt: Slip Trailing (Thrown, Slip Trailed, Feathered Dish by Joan Hotchin (YORYM-2004.1.1391))

story.hook: Drawing with liquid clay from a bottle, like icing a cake.
story.body:
Slip trailing pipes a thick slip onto leather-hard clay to make raised lines, dots and patterns. It is the technique of English slipware, of Thomas Toft's great dishes, and of everyday pottery across Europe and Japan.

A soft bulb or squeeze bottle with a fine nozzle and a slip the consistency of thick cream are all it needs; the line has a lively, wobbly energy that is hard to fake.
story.reflection: What would you draw if the line could not be erased?

techniques.tryIt: Trail white slip onto a dark, leather-hard plate and finish with a clear or honey glaze.

techniques.name: Nerikomi / Neriage
techniques.visualCaption: Colored clay layered, stretched, revealed.

story.hook: Stacking and slicing coloured clays so the pattern runs right through the wall.
story.body:
Nerikomi, a Japanese term, means building with clays of different colours, layered, rolled and sliced like millefiori glass, so the pattern is in the body itself, not on the surface. It is related to agateware in England.

It needs clays that shrink at the same rate, usually one base clay coloured with stains or oxides, and patience: sliced pieces are pressed into moulds or built into slabs.
story.reflection: What does a pattern mean when it goes all the way through?

techniques.tryIt: Colour one white body with two or three stains, layer them into a block, slice it and press the slices into a simple bowl mould.

techniques.name: Terra Sigillata
techniques.visualCaption: The finest particles. Ancient Roman shine.

story.hook: The finest part of clay, brushed on and polished to a soft shine.
story.body:
Terra sigillata is a slip made from only the finest clay particles, separated by letting a watery slip settle and pouring off the top layer. Brushed on bone-dry clay and buffed with a soft cloth, it gives a satin sheen without glaze. The Romans used a red version on their tableware, and it is widely used today for pit, saggar and smoke firing.

Like burnishing, its shine holds best in low firings.
story.reflection: What happens when you use only the finest part of a material?

techniques.tryIt: Make terra sig from a red clay with a little deflocculant, let it settle for a day, siphon off the middle layer and brush three thin coats.

techniques.name: Mishima / Inlay
techniques.visualCaption: Carve, fill, scrape back. Patterns embedded.

image.alt: Mishima / Inlay (Korean - Tea Bowl - Walters 492097 - Profile)
image.credit: Anonymous ( Korea ) Unknown author / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: Inlaid lines: carve into clay, fill with slip, scrape back.
story.body:
Mishima is the Japanese name for the inlay technique of Korean buncheong and Goryeo celadon. Fine lines are incised in leather-hard clay, filled with a contrasting slip, and the surface is scraped clean once it firms, leaving crisp lines flush with the surface.

It makes drawing look printed and permanent, and works beautifully under clear and celadon glazes.
story.reflection: How does a line change when it sits inside the surface rather than on it?

techniques.tryIt: Incise with a fine needle tool, brush slip over the lines, wait until it is leather-hard, then scrape back with a metal rib.

techniques.name: Ash Glazing
techniques.visualCaption: Local trees become local glazes.

story.hook: Turning the ash of a fire into glaze.
story.body:
Wood ash is rich in calcium, potassium and some silica and phosphorus, so at high temperatures it melts into glass. Ash glazes, often about half ash and half clay or feldspar, give greens, ambers and runs that recall wood-fired pots, and every batch is different depending on the tree and how the ash was washed.

Washing removes the caustic soluble salts; always wear gloves and a mask when handling ash.
story.reflection: What would a glaze made from your own fireplace look like?

techniques.tryIt: Collect hardwood ash, soak and sieve it, dry it, then test it 50/50 with a clay and again with feldspar at cone 6 and cone 10.

techniques.name: Raku Firing
techniques.visualCaption: Hot from the kiln. Smoke and metal.

story.hook: Pulling red-hot pots from the kiln and smoking them in sawdust.
story.body:
Raku began in 16th-century Kyoto with tea bowls fired quickly and pulled from the kiln. American potters, led by Paul Soldner in the 1960s, added post-firing reduction: hot pots go into a can of sawdust or paper, which flames, then is closed. Glazes crackle and the cracks turn black, and copper glazes flash with metallic lustre.

It is fast, theatrical and outdoors, and needs a clay body that tolerates thermal shock. Pots are decorative, not for food.
story.reflection: What does speed bring out that a slow firing hides?

techniques.tryIt: Many Bay Area studios run raku nights; bring bisqued pots in a raku-friendly body and try a white crackle and a copper matte.

techniques.name: Soda Firing
techniques.visualCaption: Sodium vapor creates the glaze.

story.hook: A gentler cousin of salt firing: soda sprayed into a hot kiln.
story.body:
In soda firing, soda ash or bicarbonate dissolved in water is sprayed into the kiln near peak temperature. The sodium vapour flashes across the pots and glazes the exposed surfaces with an orange-peel sheen and warm flashing, like salt but with less corrosive fumes.

Slips and the clay itself play a big role, and pots facing the spray ports get the most glaze.
story.reflection: How would you design a pot to catch a moving vapour?

techniques.tryIt: Look for studios with a soda kiln that open firings to members; use flashing slips on the outside and a liner glaze inside.

techniques.name: Anagama Firing
techniques.visualCaption: The dragon kiln. Multi-day flames.

image.alt: Anagama Firing (Scott Meyers at Anagama firing (2517048572))

story.hook: A single-chamber tunnel kiln dug into a hillside, fired with wood for days.
story.body:
The anagama, 'cave kiln', came to Japan from Korea around the 5th century and was the kiln of the six ancient kilns, Shigaraki, Bizen and the rest. Its long, sloping chamber lets the flame and ash travel the whole length, so pots near the firebox are heavy with ash while those at the back are dry and flashed.

Firings last several days to more than a week; there are anagamas in Northern California run by groups of potters.
story.reflection: What would you make for a single firing that took a week?

techniques.tryIt: Ask Bay Area wood-firing groups about joining a crew; first-timers usually stoke, load and learn before putting in their own pots.

techniques.name: Wheel Throwing
techniques.visualCaption: Centrifugal force shapes the clay.

story.hook: Centring clay on a spinning wheel and pulling it up into a form.
story.body:
The potter's wheel has been used for about 5,000 years. Throwing is a sequence: centre the clay, open it, pull the walls up in a few passes, shape, and trim the foot when leather-hard. It allows fast, thin, symmetrical forms, and endless repetition, which is why it carries most functional pottery.

The kick wheel of the Leach tradition and the electric wheel of most studios work the same way; speed and water are the main variables.
story.reflection: What do you learn from making the same form a hundred times?

techniques.tryIt: Throw ten cylinders of the same weight in a session and cut one in half to check your wall thickness.

techniques.name: Press Molding
techniques.visualCaption: Clay pressed into forms.

story.hook: Pressing slabs of clay into or over a mould to repeat a form.
story.body:
Press moulding is one of the oldest ways of making in multiples: clay is pressed into a bisque or plaster mould, or draped over a hump mould, and released as it stiffens. Roman lamps, Mesoamerican figures and Japanese dishes were all made this way.

It allows square and irregular shapes that would be hard on a wheel, and lets a hand-built form be repeated.
story.reflection: Which of your hand-built forms deserve to be repeated?

techniques.tryIt: Carve a shallow dish shape in a block of clay, bisque it, and use it as a press mould for a series of plates.

techniques.name: Slip Casting
techniques.visualCaption: Liquid clay poured into plaster.

image.alt: Slip Casting (Lovers, unidentified, porcelain - Musei Capitolini - Rome, Italy - DSC05956)

story.hook: Pouring liquid clay into a plaster mould to make identical pieces.
story.body:
In slip casting, a deflocculated clay slip is poured into a plaster mould; the plaster draws water from the slip, leaving a layer of clay on the wall. After a set time the excess is poured out, and the piece is released once it stiffens. It is how most industrial porcelain and many design objects are made.

It rewards precise mould making and is ideal for thin, crisp forms that would be hard to throw.
story.reflection: How does making in multiples change what one object means?

techniques.tryIt: Start with a two-part plaster mould of a simple cup and a commercial casting slip.

techniques.name: Smoke Firing / Saggar
techniques.visualCaption: Smoke and combustibles mark the surface.

story.hook: Blackening and patterning bare clay with smoke.
story.body:
Smoke firing exposes bisqued, often burnished or terra sigillata-coated pots to smoke from sawdust, paper, leaves or horse hair, in a pit, a barrel or a saggar. Carbon soaks into the porous surface in blacks and greys, and resists such as tape or clay slip make patterns.

The pots stay porous and are for display, sealed with wax if needed.
story.reflection: What patterns would smoke draw on your work if you let it?

techniques.tryIt: A metal trash can with holes, sawdust and newspaper makes a simple smoke kiln; try horse hair on a hot, burnished pot.

techniques.name: Oxide Wash
techniques.visualCaption: Color wiped across texture.

story.hook: Rubbing raw metal oxides into texture to bring it to life.
story.body:
An oxide wash is a thin mix of a colouring oxide, usually iron, manganese or copper, with water, brushed into a bisqued or raw surface and wiped back. The oxide stays in the recesses and highlights texture, carving and impressions, and can be fired bare or under a glaze.

Use a mask when handling oxides, and keep manganese washes off food surfaces.
story.reflection: What texture on your work is waiting to be seen?

techniques.tryIt: Brush red iron oxide and water into a textured bisque tile, wipe the high points with a damp sponge, and fire it with and without a clear glaze.

ideas.name: Wabi-Sabi
ideas.visualCaption: Beauty in imperfection. The crack, the asymmetry, the worn edge.

story.hook: Beauty in what is imperfect, incomplete and passing.
story.body:
Wabi-sabi is a Japanese way of seeing, shaped by Zen Buddhism and the tea ceremony. Wabi once meant the loneliness of living apart from society and came to mean quiet, simple rusticity; sabi is the beauty of age and wear. Together they value the uneven rim, the crack, the patina and the asymmetry over the perfect and new.

Tea masters such as Sen no Rikyū in the 16th century chose rough local bowls over flawless Chinese porcelain, and Raku and Shigaraki pots became its emblems.
story.reflection: What in your work becomes more beautiful with use and age?

ideas.tryIt: Make a bowl in one sitting and resist correcting it; live with it for a week before you judge it.

links.label: Wabi-Sabi for Artists, Designers, Poets & Philosophers, Leonard Koren (Open Library)

ideas.name: Working with Local Materials
ideas.visualCaption: What can you make from what's beneath your feet?
ideas.keyQuestion: What clay is in your place? What trees could become ash?

image.alt: Working with Local Materials (Julian Martinez digging clay in the early 1920s)
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: Clay, ash and stone from where you are, so the pot belongs to its place.
story.body:
For most of history, potters used what was underfoot: the local clay, ash from their own fires, stone from the nearest hill. That is why Shigaraki looks like Shigaraki and La Chamba like La Chamba. Studio potters from Leach and Cardew to today's wild-clay movement have returned to digging, testing and processing their own materials.

It is slower and less predictable than buying a bag, and it gives work a sense of place that commercial bodies cannot. Many potters now mix the two: a reliable bought body with a local slip, ash or stone in the glaze.
story.reflection: What is underfoot where you live now?

ideas.tryIt: Keep a commercial body for the work you sell and test one local material at a time in your glazes: wood ash, a river sand, a crushed stone.

ideas.name: The Beauty of Use
ideas.visualCaption: A bowl worn smooth by ten thousand meals.
ideas.keyQuestion: How does use transform an object?

story.hook: A pot becomes beautiful by being used, every day, for years.
story.body:
Yanagi Sōetsu, founder of the Mingei movement, wrote of yō no bi, the beauty of use: the idea that ordinary objects made for daily life, by unknown hands, could be more beautiful than art objects because they served people honestly. A rice bowl's worth is measured in thousands of meals.

It is a quiet challenge to make work that asks to be handled, washed and reached for, rather than looked at.
story.reflection: Which pot in your kitchen do you reach for first, and why?

ideas.tryIt: Use your own mug for a month and note what you would change: weight, handle, rim, foot.

links.label: The Unknown Craftsman, Soetsu Yanagi (Open Library)

ideas.name: Collaborating with Fire
ideas.visualCaption: Potter makes pot, fire finishes it.
ideas.keyQuestion: What might you surrender to the kiln?

story.hook: The kiln as a partner, not a tool.
story.body:
In wood, soda, salt and raku firings, the fire leaves marks the potter cannot fully plan: ash deposits, flashing, smoke and cracks. Many potters think of the firing as the last collaborator in the making, and design their pots to receive the fire, leaving bare clay where flame will touch, placing them in the kiln by intuition.

It asks for trust and for a willingness to accept results that surprise you.
story.reflection: Where in your process do you leave room for something other than you?

ideas.tryIt: Put the same form in three different spots in a firing and compare what each place gave it.

ideas.name: Constraint as Creativity
ideas.keyQuestion: What might you make with only what you have?

story.hook: Limits that make the work better.
story.body:
Many great pottery traditions grew from limits: one clay, one kiln, one form repeated thousands of times. Constraints force invention: Korean buncheong potters, with grey clay and no porcelain, invented a whole language of white slip; Mingei potters made beauty within the needs of everyday use.

In the studio, a self-imposed limit, one glaze, one form, one day, often opens more doors than a free hand.
story.reflection: What single limit would most help your work right now?

ideas.tryIt: Choose one clay and one glaze for a month and see how far you can push them.

ideas.name: The Sacred Everyday
ideas.keyQuestion: What daily ritual deserves a beautiful vessel?

image.credit: Association of Cultural Properties / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: The cup, the bowl, the plate: the most intimate art there is.
story.body:
Daily objects touch the lips, sit in the hand and come back again and again. They have to work: hold heat, pour cleanly, stack, wash, feel right. Within those demands, potters have found endless variety, from a Song tea bowl to a Hamada plate to a market jug.

The daily object is where craft meets life, and where a potter's sensitivity shows most in small things: the weight, the rim, the foot.
story.reflection: What daily object would you most like to perfect?

ideas.tryIt: Pick one form you use every day and make twelve of them, changing only one thing each time.

ideas.name: Time Made Visible
ideas.visualCaption: Every pot is a record of its making.
ideas.keyQuestion: What marks of time does your work carry?

story.hook: Clay records time: the hand, the drying, the fire and the years of use.
story.body:
A pot carries traces of every stage of its making: the throwing rings, the trimming, the fingerprints, the way it slumped in the fire. Then it keeps recording, as surfaces wear, crazing darkens and repairs accumulate. Archaeologists read whole civilisations in potsherds because clay outlasts almost everything.

Working with clay is a slow conversation with time: you cannot rush drying, and the kiln has its own schedule.
story.reflection: What do you want your pots to remember about you?

ideas.tryIt: Leave one stage visible on purpose: the throwing lines, the coil joins, the cut marks.

ideas.name: Anonymous Making
ideas.keyQuestion: What could you make if you didn't sign it?

story.hook: Beauty made by people whose names were never recorded.
story.body:
Most of the world's great pottery was made by people whose names we do not know. Yanagi Sōetsu argued in The Unknown Craftsman that unsigned, everyday work, made by hand without self-consciousness, could reach a beauty that individual artists strive for. Hamada famously did not sign his pots.

The idea asks what it would mean to make work where skill, not identity, is what shows.
story.reflection: Would you make differently if no one would ever know it was yours?

ideas.tryIt: Make a set you will not sign, give it away, and notice whether it changes how you make it.

links.label: The Unknown Craftsman, Soetsu Yanagi (Open Library)

ideas.name: Tradition and Innovation
ideas.keyQuestion: How does tradition enable rather than constrain?

story.hook: Every new thing in clay begins inside an old one.
story.body:
Potters have always worked between inheritance and invention. Korean potters taken to Japan founded new traditions; Maria Martinez revived a lost San Ildefonso black ware and changed it; Peter Voulkos took the functional jar and broke it open into sculpture. Tradition gives a vocabulary, and innovation comes from knowing it well enough to change it.

The question is not whether to follow or break tradition but which one you belong to and what you add.
story.reflection: Which tradition do you speak, and what would you add to it?

ideas.tryIt: Choose one historical form that moves you and make five versions, each one further from the original.

ideas.name: Truth to Materials
ideas.keyQuestion: What does the material want to do?

image.alt: Truth to Materials (Ian Sprague spheroidal stoneware vase St Kilda 1-12-2015)

story.hook: Let clay be clay: show what the material is, not what it imitates.
story.body:
Truth to materials is the idea that a work should honour the nature of what it is made from rather than disguise it. It grew out of John Ruskin and William Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement in 19th-century Britain, which rejected the machine-made imitation of one material by another. Later, sculptors such as Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth made it a modernist principle.

In ceramics, Bernard Leach and the Mingei potters made it central: clay that shows its grit, glazes from natural materials, forms that come from the wheel and the hand rather than from imitating metal or glass. Michael Cardew carried it into his work in Ghana and Nigeria.
story.reflection: What does your clay want to do, if you let it?

ideas.tryIt: Leave the outside of a pot bare, or with one thin slip, and let the clay's colour and grain be the surface.

ideas.name: Slow Making
ideas.keyQuestion: What might you achieve with ten times more time?

story.hook: Making at the pace the material asks for.
story.body:
Clay sets its own rhythm: it must dry slowly, be trimmed at the right moment, be fired over hours or days. The slow-making movement, like slow food, values that pace against speed and volume, and the attention it builds.

Many potters find that the slowest parts, wedging, waiting, trimming, are where their attention and ideas come.
story.reflection: Which step of your process would you like to slow down?

ideas.tryIt: Choose one piece a week to make with no deadline, and give it as long as it needs at each stage.

ideas.name: The Space Between
ideas.visualCaption: Neither purely useful nor purely decorative.
ideas.keyQuestion: Where does function end and art begin?

story.hook: When a vessel is also a sculpture, and a sculpture still holds something.
story.body:
The line between a useful pot and a sculpture has long been blurred. Song dynasty vases, Bizen flower vessels, Hans Coper's spade forms and Peter Voulkos's stacked jars all hold space and suggest use while being chiefly about form.

Functional sculpture keeps the vessel's logic, an opening, an inside and outside, while freeing it from daily duty.
story.reflection: What if a pot only had to hold a single stem, or only air?

ideas.tryIt: Throw a vessel and then cut, alter and reassemble it, keeping one opening so it is still a vessel.

moments.name: The Korean Invasions (1592-98)
moments.visualCaption: Hundreds of Korean potters taken to Japan—transforming both countries' ceramics forever.
moments.significance: Created Hagi, Karatsu, Arita traditions; ended Korean buncheong

image.alt: The Korean Invasions (1592-98) (Aichi Prefectural Ceramic Museum (38))

story.hook: A war that moved a whole ceramic tradition from one country to another.
story.body:
Toyotomi Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea in 1592 and 1597 are sometimes called the 'pottery wars'. Japanese warlords, eager for the tea ceremony, took hundreds of Korean potters back to Japan, where they founded or transformed the kilns of Hagi, Karatsu, Satsuma and Arita, and found porcelain stone at Arita around 1616.

In Korea the loss, along with destruction of kilns, helped end buncheong production. Some Korean families have worked in Japan as potters for over four hundred years since.
story.reflection: How much of a tradition lives in the people who carry it?

moments.tryIt: Look at Karatsu and Hagi tea bowls side by side with Korean buncheong; you can see the Korean hand in both.

moments.name: Jōmon Flame Vessels Recognized
moments.visualCaption: The oldest pottery on Earth finally seen as art.
moments.significance: Challenged assumptions about 'primitive' ceramics; influenced contemporary makers

story.hook: An American zoologist digs a shell mound and names the world's oldest pottery.
story.body:
In 1877 Edward S. Morse, an American zoologist teaching in Tokyo, spotted a shell mound from a train window at Ōmori and excavated it. He found cord-marked pottery and described it as 'cord marked', which in Japanese became jōmon, giving its name to the whole period.

Later radiocarbon dates showed some Jōmon pottery to be more than 15,000 years old, among the oldest known in the world.
story.reflection: What would someone a thousand years from now read in your pots?

moments.tryIt: Press twisted cord or string into a coil-built pot while soft, as the Jōmon potters did.

moments.name: Leach Meets Hamada (1919)
moments.visualCaption: East and West meet in a Tokyo raku party.
moments.significance: Led to St Ives pottery; created studio pottery movement

image.alt: Leach Meets Hamada (1919) (The Leach Pottery, St. Ives, Cornwall - Museum Entrance)
image.credit: Jordanhill School D&T Dept / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: An English artist and a Japanese chemist-potter meet, and studio pottery is born.
story.body:
Bernard Leach went to Japan in 1909 as an etcher, took up raku pottery in Tokyo and studied under the sixth Ogata Kenzan. Around 1919 he met Shoji Hamada, a young potter trained in ceramic chemistry. In 1920 the two sailed to England together and built a kiln at St Ives.

Their partnership, with Yanagi Sōetsu's ideas behind it, linked Japanese and English pottery and shaped the studio pottery movement around the world.
story.reflection: Who could you learn from who works on the other side of the world?

moments.tryIt: Read A Potter's Book alongside Hamada's pots: you can see the conversation between them on the page.

moments.name: Voulkos at Otis (1954-59)
moments.visualCaption: A master thrower starts slashing his pots—ceramics enters the art world.
moments.significance: Broke ceramics into fine art; influenced generations

story.hook: In 1950s Los Angeles, clay broke free of the pot.
story.body:
Peter Voulkos started a ceramics department at the Los Angeles County Art Institute (later Otis) in 1954. With students and friends including Paul Soldner, John Mason, Ken Price and Billy Al Bengston, he worked through the night, throwing huge forms, tearing and stacking them, with the energy of Abstract Expressionist painting.

The work changed what clay could be in America. In 1959 Voulkos moved to UC Berkeley, where he taught for decades and helped make the Bay Area a centre of ceramic sculpture.
story.reflection: What would you make if no one expected a pot?

moments.tryIt: Throw a large form, tear into it while wet, and rebuild it into something that no longer looks thrown.

links.label: Otis College of Art and Design (Wikipedia)

moments.name: European Porcelain Discovered (1708)
moments.visualCaption: An alchemist searching for gold finds white gold instead.
moments.significance: Ended China's porcelain monopoly; transformed European ceramics

image.alt: European Porcelain Discovered (1708) (Saxonia Museum für saechsische Vaterlandskunde I 33)

story.hook: A captive alchemist discovers the secret of porcelain in Saxony.
story.body:
Europeans had tried for centuries to copy Chinese porcelain. In Dresden, Augustus the Strong of Saxony held the young alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger, who had claimed he could make gold, and set him to work with the scholar Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus. Around 1708 they made true hard-paste porcelain from kaolin.

The Meissen factory opened in 1710 in Albrechtsburg Castle, and the recipe was guarded like a state secret, though workers soon carried it to Vienna and beyond.
story.reflection: What secrets in your own work would you want to keep, and which to share?

moments.tryIt: A cone 6 porcelain body is easy to buy; compare it side by side with stoneware to feel why Europe wanted it so badly.

moments.name: Maria Martinez Develops Black-on-Black (1919)
moments.visualCaption: Ancient technique meets innovation at San Ildefonso.
moments.significance: Revived Pueblo pottery; created new art form

story.hook: A Pueblo couple revive and reinvent a black pottery that becomes famous worldwide.
story.body:
At San Ildefonso Pueblo in New Mexico, Maria Martinez and her husband Julian, working with archaeologists studying ancient sherds, developed the black-on-black ware around 1918 to 1919. Maria built and burnished the pots; Julian painted designs with a matte slip; a smothered firing with dried manure turned them black, the polished areas glossy and the painted ones matte.

Maria taught many in the Pueblo, signed her work to help the whole community's market, and became one of the best-known potters of the 20th century.
story.reflection: How could your work help the people around you make a living too?

moments.tryIt: Burnish a leather-hard pot, paint a design in matte slip, and try a smothered smoke firing.

links.label: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

moments.name: Chōjirō Creates First Raku (c. 1580)
moments.visualCaption: A tile maker's son invents a tradition for tea.
moments.significance: Created Raku tradition; established new aesthetic

image.alt: Chōjirō Creates First Raku (c. 1580) (Tea bowl, known as Suehiro, studio of Chojiro, Raku ware, Kuroraku type, Azuchi-Momoyama t)

story.hook: A tile maker in Kyoto makes tea bowls for Sen no Rikyū.
story.body:
In the 1580s Chōjirō, a roof-tile maker, began making tea bowls by hand, without a wheel, for the tea master Sen no Rikyū. They were simple, dark or red, shaped by hand and carved, fired quickly and pulled from the kiln. Toyotomi Hideyoshi is said to have given the family a seal reading 'raku', meaning enjoyment.

The Raku family still makes tea bowls in Kyoto, now in its fifteenth and sixteenth generations.
story.reflection: What would a bowl made for one particular person look like?

moments.tryIt: Pinch and carve a tea bowl by hand, with no wheel, aiming for how it feels in two hands rather than how it looks.

moments.name: Coper Joins Rie's Studio (1946)
moments.visualCaption: Two refugees, one studio—modern ceramics transformed.

story.hook: A refugee potter and a refugee assistant in a London mews.
story.body:
Lucie Rie, who fled Vienna in 1938, set up a studio in Albion Mews in London. In 1946 Hans Coper, also a refugee, came to help her make ceramic buttons. She taught him to throw, and they shared the studio until 1958, each developing a modernist language very different from Leach's rustic stoneware: thin walls, sgraffito lines, volcanic and pitted glazes.

Rie's studio was later reconstructed in the V&A.
story.reflection: Who could share your studio and change your work?

moments.tryIt: Study Rie's sgraffito lines through manganese slip on porcelain; it is a precise, attainable technique.

moments.name: The Five Great Kilns of Song
moments.visualCaption: Ceramics reaches a peak that still defines excellence.

image.alt: The Five Great Kilns of Song (Chinese - Spittoon - Walters 491585 - Profile)
image.credit: Anonymous ( China ) Unknown author / Wikimedia Commons

story.hook: The five great kilns of the Song dynasty set the standard for refinement.
story.body:
Chinese connoisseurs later named five kilns of the Song dynasty (960 to 1279) as the finest: Ru, Guan, Ge, Ding and Jun. Ru made rare, pale blue-green wares for the court; Guan and Ge are known for their crackle; Ding for ivory-white porcelain with carved decoration; Jun for thick, opalescent blue glazes splashed with purple.

Their quiet forms and glazes still guide potters who seek restraint.
story.reflection: How little decoration does a pot need?

moments.tryIt: Pick one Song form and make it in a single glaze; let the glaze thickness do all the decorating.

moments.name: Picasso Arrives in Vallauris (1946)
moments.visualCaption: A painter discovers clay—transforms a village and medium.
moments.significance: Brought fine art attention to ceramics

story.hook: At 65, Picasso falls for clay in a small Riviera workshop.
story.body:
In 1946 Picasso visited the Madoura pottery of Suzanne and Georges Ramié in Vallauris. He came back in 1947 and over the next two decades made thousands of ceramics there: plates painted as faces, vases turned into women and birds, editions produced with the workshop.

His presence revived Vallauris as a ceramics town and showed the art world that clay was a serious medium for painters and sculptors.
story.reflection: What would you do with clay if you came to it with fresh eyes?

moments.tryIt: Take a thrown form and alter it into a figure or animal while it's soft, as Picasso did with Madoura's vases.

moments.name: Yanagi Founds Mingei Movement (1926)
moments.visualCaption: A philosopher sees beauty in everyday objects.
moments.significance: Changed how we value craft; influenced global studio pottery

story.hook: A philosopher and two potters name the beauty of everyday things.
story.body:
In the mid-1920s Yanagi Sōetsu, with the potters Shoji Hamada and Kawai Kanjiro, coined the word mingei, 'art of the people', for the anonymous folk crafts of Japan and Korea. They argued that humble everyday objects made by unknown craftspeople had a beauty art had lost.

Yanagi founded the Japan Folk Crafts Museum in Tokyo in 1936, and the movement's ideas, through Leach, spread to studio potters worldwide.
story.reflection: What everyday object near you deserves a museum?

moments.tryIt: The Mingei International Museum in San Diego carries this tradition in California and is worth a visit.

links.label: The Unknown Craftsman, Soetsu Yanagi (Open Library)

moments.name: Doña Rosa's Burnishing Innovation (1950s)
moments.visualCaption: One woman transforms an ancient tradition.

story.hook: A potter in Oaxaca discovers how to make black clay shine.
story.body:
In San Bartolo Coyotepec, potters had long made matte grey-black pots from local clay fired in reduction. In the 1950s Doña Rosa Real de Nieto found that polishing the pot with quartz before firing gave it a metallic shine, and the barro negro we know today was born.

The shiny ware drew collectors and visitors from around the world, and her family's workshop still welcomes them.
story.reflection: What small change in your process might transform your work?

moments.tryIt: Polish a leather-hard red clay pot with a smooth stone and fire it in a reducing smoke firing to see the shine survive.

moments.name: Chinese Export Collapse (1640s-80s)
moments.visualCaption: When China stopped shipping, the world had to make its own.
moments.significance: Created Delft, boosted Arita, drove European porcelain quest

image.alt: Chinese Export Collapse (1640s-80s) (Table Service MET DT11573 (cropped))

story.hook: When China's porcelain stopped flowing, Japan and Delft stepped in.
story.body:
In the mid-17th century the fall of the Ming dynasty and the Qing conquest disrupted the kilns of Jingdezhen and coastal trade. The Dutch East India Company, which had shipped millions of pieces of Chinese porcelain to Europe, turned to Japan, where the young kilns of Arita filled the gap with Imari and Kakiemon wares.

In Europe, Delft potters made blue-and-white tin-glazed earthenware in imitation, and the race to make true porcelain began.
story.reflection: What becomes possible when a supply you depend on disappears?

moments.tryIt: Compare Chinese blue-and-white, Arita and Delft side by side; the same image changes completely with the clay.

moments.name: A Potter's Book Published (1940)
moments.visualCaption: The bible of studio pottery appears.
moments.significance: Defined studio pottery philosophy and practice for generations

story.hook: A book that taught generations to become potters.
story.body:
Bernard Leach published A Potter's Book in 1940. It joined practical instruction, on clay, glazes, kilns and throwing, with a philosophy of the pot as a balance of beauty and use, drawn from his years in Japan. For decades it was the first book many studio potters read.

It also set a standard of the 'good pot' that later potters both learned from and argued against.
story.reflection: What would you put in a book for someone just starting?

moments.tryIt: Read the chapter on 'Towards a Standard', then look at a few of your own pots against it, and decide where you disagree.

links.label: A Potter's Book, Bernard Leach (Open Library)

moments.name: George Ohr's Work Rediscovered (1970s)
moments.visualCaption: A mad potter's attic reveals treasures.
moments.significance: Proved prophetic vision; revalued American ceramics history

story.hook: Thousands of pots by the 'Mad Potter of Biloxi', hidden for decades, are found.
story.body:
George Ohr made wildly twisted, thin-walled, colourfully glazed pots in Biloxi, Mississippi, at the turn of the 20th century, and called himself the greatest art potter on earth. Few agreed at the time. After he stopped potting, around 1910, thousands of pieces sat stored away by his family.

In the late 1960s an antiques dealer, James Carpenter, bought the hoard, and the work was seen as decades ahead of its time. The Ohr-O'Keefe Museum of Art in Biloxi, designed by Frank Gehry, now shows it.
story.reflection: What work of yours might take years to be understood?
